**Summary.** This paper explores the theoretical limit of distinguishing non-orthogonal quantum states when classical information is available. It demonstrates that allowing queries to depend on the measurement outcome (adaptive post-measurement) can yield a higher success probability than having prior knowledge, fundamentally challenging intuition about the value of timing in quantum measurements.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses fundamental limits in quantum communication protocols by showing that measurement back-action can be leveraged optimally through adaptivity, which is crucial for understanding resource limitations in quantum sensing and cryptography.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether allowing classical information to arrive adaptively after a quantum measurement can improve the perfect discrimination of non-orthogonal quantum states compared to having that information available beforehand.

**Main result.** Adaptive post-measurement queries can, in certain cases, allow for the perfect discrimination of pairwise non-orthogonal states, surpassing limits set by pre-measurement knowledge. The optimal strategy relates this problem to standard minimum-error discrimination on an auxiliary ensemble.

**Method.** The authors develop a theoretical framework comparing success probabilities ($P_{	ext{pre}}$ vs $P_{	ext{adapt\_post}}$) and derive the optimal measurement strategy by mapping the adaptive query scenario onto a known minimum-error discrimination problem for an auxiliary ensemble ($\mathcal{E}_{	ext{aux}}$).

**Model / system.** The model is quantum state discrimination involving a set of pairwise non-orthogonal pure quantum states ($\psi_x$) in a given Hilbert space dimension ($d$). Examples include trine and tetrahedron ensembles.

**Key observables.** Success probabilities for discrimination: $P_{	ext{pre}}$ (pre-measurement), $P_{	ext{post}}$ (outcome-independent post-measurement), and $P_{	ext{adapt\_post}}$ (adaptive post-measurement query).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of states ($n$), the dimension of the Hilbert space ($d$), and the overlap between states ($\langle \psi_i | \psi_j angle$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often focuses on the case where only one bit of classical information is available, and it challenges the intuition that earlier classical information is always superior.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the timing difference between query types (red vs. blue). Figure 2 provides a graphical representation of the auxiliary ensemble for $n=4$.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares three scenarios for classical information: pre-measurement, outcome-independent post-measurement, and adaptive post-measurement queries. It establishes a general method relating the optimal adaptive strategy to minimum-error discrimination on an auxiliary ensemble.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A set of pairwise non-orthogonal quantum states cannot be perfectly discriminated, and this remains true even when one bit of classical partial information is available prior to the measurement. Contrary to the usual intuition that earlier information is at least as valuable as later information, we show that the same bit can be more useful when it arrives after the measurement. We present a framework for state discrimination in which the sender provides classical information in response to a request from the receiver, which we refer to as a query. In some cases, pairwise non-orthogonal states can be perfectly discriminated when the query is allowed to depend on the measurement outcome. We give a general method for finding the optimal strategy in this setting, which turns out to be the standard minimum-error discrimination problem for an auxiliary ensemble.

</details>

**Summary.** This research tackles the critical issue of growth-induced disorder in NV centers within diamond used for quantum sensing. By comparing pulsed versus smooth nitrogen doping methods, the authors demonstrate that controlled doping procedures are essential to minimize interfacial strain and defects. This leads to high-quality layers capable of achieving near-theoretical coherence limits and enabling sensitive NMR detection.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it directly addresses material science limitations (growth defects) that impede the realization of solid-state quantum sensors, bridging condensed matter physics with quantum optics/sensing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how growth-induced interfacial disorder, stemming from nitrogen doping procedures during CVD diamond growth, degrades the coherence of Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers.

**Main result.** Smooth nitrogen delivery significantly suppresses this interfacial disorder, leading to NV spin-coherence properties approaching theoretical limits. The work also successfully demonstrated proton NMR detection using these high-quality layers.

**Method.** The researchers compared two nitrogen injection methods (pulsed vs. smooth) and used advanced characterization techniques like ODMR spectroscopy, ToF-SIMS depth profiling, and step-etching to map disorder gradients.

**Model / system.** The physical system is NV centers embedded in $^12	ext{C}$-enriched diamond thin films grown on (111) substrates. The analysis focuses on the impact of nitrogen concentration profiles and resulting lattice strain/defects on spin coherence.

**Key observables.** NV spin-coherence decay rates ($\Gamma^*_2$, $\Gamma_{	ext{DQR}}^2$), Nitrogen concentration profiles ([N]), P1 center concentrations ([P1]), and NMR signal detection capability.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interfacial disorder magnitude, nitrogen doping procedure type (pulsed vs. smooth), effective depth ($d_{NV}$), and the resulting coherence time limit imposed by spin-bath noise.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often approximates the total decay rate as a sum of contributions ($\Gamma^*_2 \approx \Gamma_{	ext{DQR}}^2 + \Gamma_{	ext{strain}}$) and assumes certain background contributions are minor for simplification.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate OES/ToF-SIMS profiles comparing doping methods, ODMR spectra showing decay rates across etched layers (R0-R3), and final results summarizing concentration gradients and NMR detection signals.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares two growth procedures using multiple characterization tools (OES, ToF-SIMS) to quantify disorder. It then uses step-etching and spin-coherence measurements across depth profiles to correlate doping history with quantum performance, culminating in a demonstration of high-sensitivity sensing.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in chemical-vapor-deposition (CVD) diamond can form preferentially oriented ensembles with high sensing performance and low densities of lattice defects. Thin films of this material are a cornerstone of various imaging modalities. However, nitrogen injection needed to produce such films can transiently drive growth out of equilibrium, generating interfacial strain and spin defects that degrade NV coherence. Here, we investigate this disorder in $^{12}\text{C}$-enriched, preferentially oriented NV layers grown on (111) diamond using two nitrogen-injection procedures, combined with nanometer-scale selective plasma etching and NV spin-coherence measurements. Pulsed nitrogen injection produces a pronounced nitrogen overshoot within a 60--80 nm interfacial region, generating excessive amounts of defects. By contrast, smooth nitrogen delivery through mass flow controllers substantially suppresses interfacial disorder, yielding coherence properties close to the theoretical limit imposed by spin-bath noise. A 50-nm NV layer is used to demonstrate proton nuclear magnetic resonance detection. This work reveals the role of interfacial disorder associated with the nitrogen-doping procedure and provides a route to growing high-quality, thin NV-doped layers for quantum-sensing applications.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper revisits the thermal limits of superconducting quantum computers by developing an advanced heat estimation model. It demonstrates that previously overlooked heat sources, particularly from readout amplifiers and wiring resistance, create a dominant thermal bottleneck. The findings are critical for designing viable, large-scale cryogenic quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses hardware limitations in scaling quantum computation, which is crucial for any theoretical physicist working on open quantum systems or building complex quantum architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The readout amplification chain imposes a critical thermal scalability bottleneck that limits the size of superconducting quantum processors.

**Main result.** Amplifier-associated heat emerges as the dominant thermal bottleneck in modern large-scale cryogenic systems, requiring new modeling approaches to predict true qubit capacity.

**Method.** The authors developed an improved system-level thermal estimation model that fully accounts for active dissipation, passive conduction, and Joule heating across multiple cryogenic stages.

**Model / system.** The study models superconducting quantum processors housed in a dilution refrigerator (DR) with distinct temperature stages ($	ext{RT}$ down to $\sim 10	ext{ mK}$). The model calculates the total normalized heat load by summing contributions from cables, attenuators, and amplifiers.

**Key observables.** Total Normalized Heat Load ($	ext{NHL}_{	ext{THL},s}$) at each cryogenic stage; maximum supported physical qubit capacity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Active dissipation, passive conduction coefficients, Joule heating resistance/currents, target scale (e.g., 10k qubits).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Previous models are criticized for omitting or underestimating the combined heat load from the readout amplifier chain, leading to overestimation of scalability.

**Figures summary.** Figure 2 compares two scalability trends: one dominated by passive heat load (SS wiring) and a second showing bottleneck migration towards the $4	ext{ K}$ stage with modern components.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the thermal bottleneck problem, details the improved unified modeling framework incorporating all major heat sources, analyzes cross-technology trade-offs, and concludes by evaluating pathways toward large single-fridge systems.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The readout amplification chain imposes a critical thermal scalability bottleneck in large-scale superconducting quantum systems. This happens through three mechanisms: amplifier dissipation, passive conduction through bias wiring and Joule heating within that same wiring. These terms are absent or only partially represented in several prior system-level thermal-scalability models, leading to bottleneck misidentification and scalability overestimation. In this work, we improve upon previous system-level heat estimation models by fully accounting for the major heat sources in modern cryogenic quantum systems including the active dissipation, passive conduction, and Joule heating in the readout amplifier module. Our analysis demonstrates that amplifier-associated heat emerges as the dominant thermal bottleneck that fundamentally alters the thermal landscape of modern large-scale cryogenic systems. We explore various technology options and their tradeoffs to identify configurations that reduce this critical heat load and improve scalability. Finally, we evaluate forward-looking system configurations, including larger refrigeration platforms and optical approaches, and analyze forward-looking pathways toward single-fridge 10k-qubit cryogenic systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the entanglement structure of the 1D repulsive Hubbard model by examining the reduced density matrix after partitioning one spin species. The authors find that this leads to a modular Luttinger liquid whose correlations are governed by a single effective parameter, $\sqrt{K_c K_s}$. This demonstrates a universal principle: even when tracing out degrees of freedom, the entanglement structure retains critical algebraic correlations characteristic of 1D quantum liquids.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of an 'entanglement Hamiltonian' provides a powerful tool to characterize entanglement in interacting quantum systems. Finding that this modular structure is robust and yields a simple geometric mean for the correlation parameter offers deep insights into how entanglement encodes underlying symmetries, which is relevant for understanding exotic phases in correlated materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to determine the universal low-energy entanglement Hamiltonian associated with a spin partition in an interacting one-dimensional metal, specifically investigating its structure when tracing out one spin species from the Hubbard model.

**Main result.** Tracing out one spin species yields a modular Luttinger liquid whose effective correlation is governed by a single parameter equal to the geometric mean of the charge and spin Luttinger parameters. This reveals a universal modular structure in 1D fermionic systems.

**Method.** The authors combine bosonization techniques with exact diagonalization (ED) methods to calculate the reduced density matrix for one spin species, leading to the definition and analysis of an entanglement Hamiltonian.

**Model / system.** The primary system is the one-dimensional repulsive Hubbard model. The analysis proceeds by mapping the interacting fermionic problem onto bosonic fields via bosonization, allowing for the calculation of entanglement properties.

**Key observables.** Entanglement entropy, entanglement spectrum (eigenvalues of $H_{	ext{ent}}$), and Luttinger parameters ($K_c, K_s$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The effective single LL parameter $\sqrt{K_c K_s}$, the repulsive interaction strength $U$, and the hopping amplitude $t$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on bosonization techniques and assumes that the reduced density matrix is Gaussian-structured, which is valid for the quadratic nature of the bosonized theory.

**Figures summary.** Figures visualize the universal branching hierarchy in the entanglement spectrum (Fig. 1) and show the evolution of the entanglement density of states compared to bosonization predictions (Fig. 2).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by defining the reduced density matrix for one spin species ($ho_\uparrow$) and deriving the associated entanglement Hamiltonian ($H_{	ext{mod}}$). It then applies this formalism to the Hubbard model, using bosonization results to predict universal properties like the effective Luttinger parameter and the branching structure of the spectrum.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the spin-partitioned entanglement Hamiltonian of the one-dimensional repulsive Hubbard model. By combining bosonization with exact diagonalization, we show that tracing out one spin species produces a modular Luttinger liquid, whose properties fundamentally differ from those of the physical system. While the modular spectrum is fully dispersionless and possesses a momentum-independent entanglement gap, its eigenstates exhibit algebraic correlations governed by a single effective Luttinger parameter equal to the geometric mean of the charge and spin Luttinger parameters. The resulting entanglement spectrum displays a universal branching hierarchy in excellent agreement with exact diagonalization. We further demonstrate that the modular ground state is nearly identical to that of the spinless Luttinger liquid. These results uncover a universal modular structure in interacting one-dimensional fermionic systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents Oraqle, a comprehensive framework to benchmark the entire readout-to-QEC pipeline for superconducting qubits. It systematically analyzes how measurement duration, machine learning discriminators, and QEC codes interact to determine the final logical error rate. The key takeaway is that hardware optimization should focus on reducing readout latency rather than over-engineering the classical decoding model.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides concrete, quantitative guidelines for optimizing the physical implementation layer (readout electronics and ML) that directly impacts the theoretical performance limits of fault-tolerant quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The performance of Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is critically dependent on the readout process, but this co-dependence between readout characteristics, ML discriminators, and QEC performance has not been deeply studied.

**Main result.** The study reveals that measurement duration can be significantly reduced with minimal logical error rate penalty, and discriminator complexity is largely irrelevant as residual errors are dominated by device physics.

**Method.** The authors introduce Oraqle, an end-to-end benchmarking framework that systematically evaluates the entire pipeline from raw qubit readout traces through ML discrimination to final QEC performance metrics.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on superconducting qubits operating in the dispersive regime. The system involves a full cycle: ancilla readout $ightarrow$ ML decoding $ightarrow$ error correction, tested across multiple QEC codes (e.g., Surface, Color).

**Key observables.** Logical Error Rate (LER), Readout Fidelity ($F_{5Q}$), and the raw IQ trace data used for classification.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Measurement duration ($\mu$s scale), discriminator complexity/model size, and the specific QEC code structure.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis compares current hardware limitations with projected device capabilities across various noise models (e.g., decoherence-only vs. full flip error).

**Figures summary.** Figures compare LER versus measurement duration under different noise assumptions, demonstrating that readout flip errors are the primary driver of performance degradation at short timescales.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the QEC cycle and identifies readout as a bottleneck; it then introduces Oraqle to benchmark the entire stack across multiple codes and hardware regimes, culminating in three key findings regarding measurement time, discriminator role, and maturity dependence.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum error correction (QEC) is the most promising route toward fault-tolerant quantum computing and, thus, useful quantum computers. QEC operates as a continuous measure-decode-correct cycle: ancilla qubits are read out, a decoder infers errors from the resulting syndromes, and corrections are applied before the next round begins. Within this loop, readout occupies a uniquely critical role, as it is the sole source of ground truth available to the decoder. Yet readout is also the slowest and most error-prone operation in the stack, with characteristics that vary across qubits and drift over time; This complexity propagates directly to the classical control hardware, and in particular to the FPGA-hosted machine-learning (ML) discriminator that must classify each analog signal into a binary syndrome outcome. Despite this central role, QEC performance has not yet been studied in depth from the perspective of readout characteristics, readout length, and their co-design with an ML discriminator.   We introduce Oraqle, an end-to-end benchmarking framework that evaluates qubit-state readout and its impact on QEC performance across real experimentally extracted qubit-state-readout datasets, state-of-the-art ML discriminators, multiple QEC codes, and hardware regimes spanning current to projected devices. Our study reveals three asymmetric findings: The measurement duration can be significantly reduced with nearly no penalty to the logical error rate; The discriminator complexity barely affects the QEC performance, as residual errors are written into device physics rather than the model; and the impact of qubit-state readout on the logical error rate is conditional on where the hardware sits in the QEC landscape, a window that widens as devices mature.

</details>

**Summary.** The research presents a method to create compact, high-efficiency nonlinear optical devices by integrating Gallium Nitride (GaN) hole-type circular Bragg grating cavities onto standard optical fibers. By leveraging the cavity's resonant enhancement and directional coupling, they achieved significantly boosted Second-Harmonic Generation signals. This establishes a practical and scalable platform for incorporating strong nonlinearity into fiber-based quantum and classical photonic systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it provides a solid platform for generating strong nonlinear light sources (like entangled photons or frequency-converted light) directly within standard telecom fibers, which is crucial for building quantum communication networks.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge is achieving compact and efficient frequency conversion, specifically Second-Harmonic Generation (SHG), within optical fibers for advanced nonlinear and quantum photonic technologies.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated a scalable approach by integrating a Gallium Nitride (GaN) hole-type circular Bragg grating (h-CBG) cavity directly onto an optical fiber, achieving drastically enhanced SHG signals.

**Method.** They utilized deterministic pick-and-place transfer techniques to integrate the fabricated GaN h-CBG membrane cavity onto a standard fiber core and characterized performance using pulsed laser spectroscopy.

**Model / system.** The physical system is an all-fiber integrated nonlinear device based on a GaN h-CBG structure. This grating acts as a resonant cavity, confining light fields to enhance the second-order nonlinear susceptibility ($\chi^2$) interaction for SHG generation.

**Key observables.** SHG signal enhancement factor (up to $\sim 32	imes$ vs. freestanding membrane), resonance wavelength ($\approx 784 	ext{ nm}$), and power-normalized conversion efficiency ($3.62 	imes 10^{-3} 	ext{ W}^{-1}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** GaN material properties, cavity geometry parameters (e.g., radial period $r$, hole size $a$), and pump wavelength ($\approx 784 	ext{ nm}$ for SHG at $\lambda/2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The efficiency calculations rely on estimating peak intensity from average power measurements using the known pulse characteristics of the Ti:Sapphire laser.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the device schematic, simulated far-field radiation patterns showing directional out-coupling, measured cavity mode spectra confirming resonance at $784 	ext{ nm}$, and setups detailing both SHG measurement and the deterministic fiber transfer process.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the fabrication of GaN h-CBG membranes via etching, characterizes the resonant optical properties using spectroscopy, demonstrates the high efficiency of SHG generation within the cavity structure, and concludes with a successful demonstration of robust, in-line integration onto an optical fiber platform.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Compact and efficient frequency conversion within optical fibers is highly desirable for nonlinear and quantum photonic technologies, yet it remains challenging due to weak nonlinear interactions and limited coupling efficiencies onto optical fibers. Here, we demonstrate resonantly enhanced second-harmonic generation (SHG) through the all-fiber integration of a gallium nitride (GaN) hole-type circular Bragg grating (h-CBG) cavity, directly transferred onto a standard optical fiber. Together with the large second-order nonlinear susceptibility and wide optical transparency window of GaN, the fabricated h-CBG membrane cavity on GaN enables strong field confinement and vertically directional out-coupling of the generated SHG signal. As a result, we observe drastically enhanced SHG signals from the h-CBG device compared with the bulk GaN and the unpatterned freestanding GaN membrane. Using a deterministic pick-and-place transfer technique, we demonstrate robust and precise fiber integration of the GaN cavity device, enabling in-line SHG generation from a conventional fiber platform. This work establishes a compact and scalable approach for incorporating optical nonlinearity into fiber-based photonic systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously proves that general Positive Operator-Valued Measures (POVMs) can achieve correlations strictly greater than those achievable by projective measurements (PVMs) when local dimensions are fixed. The separation is quantified using a novel Bell functional and proven analytically via advanced algebraic techniques, establishing a fundamental resource difference in quantum measurement theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly rigorous mathematical tool—an analytic Bell functional with an exact certificate—to quantify fundamental differences between measurement models in quantum information theory, which is crucial for understanding device capabilities.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to establish a rigorous, analytic separation between correlations achievable by general quantum measurements (POVMs) and those restricted to projective measurements (PVMs) in a bipartite setting.

**Main result.** An explicit qubit POVM was constructed whose Bell value strictly exceeds the upper bound derived for all possible qubit PVM strategies over arbitrary shared two-qubit states, establishing a certified gap greater than 1/1000.

**Method.** The separation is formalized using a specialized Bell functional and proven analytically through advanced mathematical techniques, including the use of exact level-3 noncommutative sum-of-squares (SOS) certificates in an algebraic framework.

**Model / system.** The study analyzes correlations in a finite bipartite setting involving shared two-qubit states ($ho_{AB}$), comparing measurement outcomes from general POVMs versus restricted PVMs on qubits.

**Key observables.** Bell functional value $B$, the quantum maximum $\Omega = 2\sqrt{2} + 1/100$, and the upper bound for qubit PVM strategies.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Local dimension (fixed vs. unrestricted), the small parameter $\epsilon$ used in constructing the separating functional, and the specific structure of the two-qubit state.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The separation is only meaningful when local dimensions are constrained; otherwise, Naimark's theorem allows dilation to remove the distinction.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the Bell scenario comparing qubit POVMs vs. qubit projective measurements using a specific functional $B$, and Table I summarizes benchmark values for different measurement types.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the physical problem (POVM vs PVM separation) to constructing an explicit separating POVM, deriving the necessary algebraic bounds via SOS certificates, and finally proving that this constructed value attains the dimension-unrestricted quantum optimum.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Generalized measurements can be implemented projectively after enlarging the Hilbert space, but this dilation changes the available local dimension. We construct a Bell functional with rational coefficients that separates the two measurement models at local dimension two. An explicit three-outcome qubit positive-operator-valued measure with rational matrix entries attains $2\sqrt2+1/100$. On the other hand, all qubit-projective strategies are bounded by $2\sqrt2+\sqrt5/250+\sqrt2/32400$, giving a fully analytic certified gap greater than $1/1000$. To our knowledge, this is the first fully analytic Bell-functional separation between qubit POVMs and qubit projective measurements over arbitrary shared two-qubit states. Lean certificate for the separation theorem is provided for completeness. Separately, an exact level-3 noncommutative sum-of-squares certificate proves that the explicit qubit strategy attains the unrestricted finite-dimensional tensor-product quantum optimum.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops an advanced framework for Quantum Error Correction Codes (QECCs) tailored specifically for $\mathbb Z_2$ Lattice Gauge Theory. It generalizes the error correction capability from single-qubit errors to arbitrary $t$-qubit errors while optimizing resource usage. The work is significant because it provides a physically motivated, highly efficient code structure that outperforms standard methods in terms of Hamiltonian locality.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit connection between lattice gauge theory constraints and robust quantum error correction provides a powerful physical realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation, which is highly relevant to building hardware simulators or actual quantum processors based on local interactions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work generalizes quantum error correction codes (QECCs) based on $\mathbb Z_2$ Gauss's law constraints from correcting single-qubit errors to being robust against arbitrary $t$-qubit errors.

**Main result.** The derived Gauss's law code excels at reducing the locality of the encoded Hamiltonian compared to domain-agnostic codes, and it reduces physical qubit overhead for small error thresholds ($t \le 3$).

**Method.** The authors derive explicit constructions for these generalized codes by combining classical GL codes with X-type classical codes, followed by detailed calculations of the logical error rate using transfer matrix methods.

**Model / system.** The physical system is $\mathbb Z_2$ Lattice Gauge Theory (LGT) coupled to matter on a lattice. The theory focuses on constructing stabilizer codes whose constraints are dictated by Gauss's law, which must be satisfied for the quantum state.

**Key observables.** Code distance ($d$), encoding rate ($k/n$), physical qubit overhead, locality of the encoded Hamiltonian, and logical error rate (LER).

**Important parameters / regimes.** $t$ (the maximum number of correlated errors corrected), $p$ (physical error rate for BSC), and lattice dimensionality (1D, 2D).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often assumes uncorrelated X/Z noise when calculating the LER, and it compares results against linear codes.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates a 1D example of $\mathbb Z_2$ LGT showing site and link variables, alongside the construction principles for classical and quantum Gauss's law codes. Tables summarize performance metrics across different code constructions.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by generalizing the error correction capability to arbitrary $t$-qubit errors. It then details the mathematical construction of the optimal Gauss's law code, followed by rigorous calculations comparing its performance (overhead, locality) against existing methods and calculating the LER for specific noise models.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

It has previously been shown by Rajput, Roggero, and Wiebe that $\mathbb Z_2$ Gauss's law constraints can be used to build efficient quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) that are robust against arbitrary single-qubit errors. In this work, we generalize the construction to be robust against arbitrary $t$-qubit errors, where $t$ is any positive integer. This includes a derivation of the optimal Gauss's law code within the considered family by minimizing the number of physical qubits required for a given code distance. Finally, we compare our codes against other efficient QECCs on metrics such as the number of physical qubits, the locality of the encoded Hamiltonian, and the logical error rate in the code capacity setting. Compared to using a domain-agnostic code for every lattice degree of freedom, we find that the Gauss's law code primarily excels at reducing the locality of the encoded Hamiltonian. Moreover, the physical qubit overhead is also reduced for $t \le 3$ (distance $d \le 7$).

</details>

**Summary.** The paper rigorously tests effective 1D models for fermionic quantum gases by comparing them against exact 3D theory. It demonstrates that while two-body physics can be captured, accurately describing three-body correlations—which arise from transverse excitations—requires explicitly incorporating higher-order terms into the Hamiltonian. This highlights a structural limitation in simple low-dimensional effective theories.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it establishes fundamental theoretical boundaries for modeling strongly interacting quantum gases confined to low dimensions, guiding the development of more accurate many-body Hamiltonians.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the limitations of using effective one-dimensional (quasi-1D) models to describe fermionic many-body physics in ultracold atomic gases.

**Main result.** Effective 1D descriptions based only on two-body interactions are insufficient; correctly modeling the system requires explicitly including emergent three-body correlations, especially near confinement-induced resonances.

**Method.** The authors benchmarked a coupled-channel approach against exact low-energy theory derived from the underlying three-dimensional problem in both weakly and strongly attractive regimes.

**Model / system.** The system involves quasi-1D fermionic gases confined in waveguides. The theoretical framework utilizes a coupled-channel Hamiltonian ($\hat{H}_{cc}$) to model interactions, comparing its predictions against exact T-matrix calculations.

**Key observables.** Two-body scattering amplitude ($f_k$), atom-dimer scattering length ($a_{AD}^{1D}$), and the emergent three-body interaction strength ($\hat{W}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Weakly attractive limit ($a_{3D} 	o 0^-$) and strongly attractive limit ($a_{3D} 	o 0^+$); transverse confinement size ($a_\perp$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on controlled approximations within the weakly and strongly attractive limits, though the structural failure suggests a need for fully non-perturbative treatment near resonances.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate effective parameters ($E_0$, $g_{1D}$, $\Gamma$) across different coupling regimes and show diagrammatic calculations of three-body scattering corrections ($\delta T_{AD}$ and $\delta T_{3b}$).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares the coupled-channel model to exact theory, first confirming success in reproducing two-body physics. It then demonstrates failures in capturing emergent three-body interactions in both weak and strong attraction limits, necessitating explicit higher-order terms.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the validity of effective one-dimensional models for quasi-1D fermionic systems by benchmarking a coupled-channel approach against the exact low-energy theory derived from the underlying three-dimensional problem in the weakly and strongly attractive limits. We show that reproducing the exact two-body scattering amplitude is insufficient to construct the correct effective low-energy theory of quasi-1D fermions. In the weakly attractive regime, it does not capture the emergent three-body interaction induced by transverse excitations. In the strongly attractive regime, it yields an atom-dimer scattering length with an incorrect dependence on the three-dimensional scattering length. These results demonstrate the limitations of effective one-dimensional descriptions based solely on two-body physics and highlight the need to explicitly include few-body correlations in quasi-1D systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This research investigates how epitaxial compressive strain can induce high-temperature superconductivity in La2PrNi2O7 thin films, mimicking the effects of high pressure. By measuring electronic properties across a range of strains, the authors demonstrate that optimal superconducting films are fundamentally electron-like, establishing a powerful platform for understanding correlation physics beyond simple structural analogies.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides an experimental platform for tuning electronic correlations in strongly correlated materials using strain, which is analogous to external fields used in quantum simulation or theoretical modeling of interacting electron systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To test whether high-temperature superconductivity (HTS) in nickelates is induced by compressive strain, mimicking hydrostatic pressure, or if the underlying electronic mechanism differs.

**Main result.** The superconducting films are intrinsically electron-like (negative Hall coefficient), contrasting with hole-like bulk crystals, suggesting that tuning the correlation landscape via strain is key to HTS.

**Method.** Systematic epitaxial growth of La2PrNi2O7 thin films on various substrates inducing controlled strain, followed by transport and magnetic characterization.

**Model / system.** The physical system is bilayer nickelate superconductors (La2PrNi2O7) grown epitaxially. The study varies the lattice mismatch to create a continuum of compressive and tensile strains, allowing comparison with bulk high-pressure data.

**Key observables.** Superconducting transition temperatures ($T_c$), Hall coefficient ($R_H$), normal state resistivity exponent ($n$), and superconducting critical fields ($	ext{H}_{c2}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Strain magnitude (from -2.14% to +0.91%), in-plane lattice constant ($a_p$), out-of-plane ratio ($c/a_p$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The superconducting mechanism is governed by the suppression of Spin Density Waves (SDW) and that strain tuning provides a valid, controllable analogue to hydrostatic pressure.

**Figures summary.** Figures detail transport ($ho$ vs $T$) showing $T_{c,	ext{onset}}$ and zero resistance; magnetic susceptibility confirming the Meissner effect; and structural data mapping lattice parameters across the strain continuum.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the platform using extreme compression on NAO substrates, systematically varies strain across multiple substrates (NAO, SLAO, LAO, LSAT), measures transport/magnetic properties, compares results to bulk high-pressure findings, and concludes by defining a structural phase diagram based on lattice parameters.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The realization of high-temperature superconductivity in bilayer nickelates under epitaxial compressive strain is widely interpreted as mimicking the effects of high hydrostatic pressure. To test the equivalence of these mechanisms, we investigated a comprehensive strain continuum ranging from compressive (-2.14%) to tensile (+0.91%). Crucially, via ozone-assisted atomic-layer epitaxy, we realized high-temperature superconductivity in as-grown La2PrNi2O7 films on NdAlO3 substrates, which induce the most extreme compressive strain in this material system. Under extreme compression (-2.14%), these films exhibit a Tc_onset of 60 K, zero resistance at 33 K, and a diamagnetic response at 20 K, with magnetotransport measurements confirming a quasi-two-dimensional superconducting nature. Comparing our phase diagram with reported data reveals distinct lattice responses: unlike in pressurized crystals, the superconducting window in epitaxial films diverges significantly in the out-of-plane parameter c (or c/ap ratio) but remains consistent with the bulk regarding the in-plane parameter ap. Crucially, while superconductivity in both systems emerges from the suppression of spin-density waves (SDW), Hall measurements reveal a fundamental electronic dichotomy: optimal superconducting films are intrinsically electron-like (exhibiting a negative Hall coefficient), in stark contrast to the hole-like nature (positive Hall coefficient) of high-pressure bulk crystals and non-superconducting tensile films. Ultimately, both tuning strategies effectively modulate the underlying correlation landscape - the true driver of superconductivity - transcending the constraints of specific Fermi surface topologies. This work establishes a macroscopic platform for probing the multi-orbital physics of nickelates, offering a new dimension for investigating high-temperature superconductivity.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper achieves the complete existence classification for absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states involving seven qudits. It proves that such states exist for all local dimensions $d \ge 3$. The proof combines novel constructions for various dimensional forms with rigorous mathematical analysis of state marginals.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a definitive classification result for a specific, highly structured class of multi-partite entangled states, which has deep connections to quantum error correction codes and the fundamental limits of entanglement in multipartite systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to establish a complete existence classification for absolutely maximally entangled states (AME) involving seven qudits, denoted $	ext{AME}(7, d)$.

**Main result.** The authors prove that an AME state of seven qudits exists if and only if the local dimension $d$ satisfies $d \ge 3$.

**Method.** The proof involves constructing specific quantum states (cyclic quadratic-phase states for odd $d$, coupled binary–odd-dimensional constructions for $d \equiv 2 \pmod 4$) and analyzing the vanishing of cross-terms in the three-party marginals using character orthogonality.

**Model / system.** The system under study is a multi-partite quantum state involving seven qudits, whose entanglement properties are characterized by the existence of AME states. These states are mathematically linked to pure quantum MDS codes with parameters $[[7, 0, \lfloor 7/2 floor + 1]]_d$.

**Key observables.** The three-party marginal $ho_S$ is a key observable; its proof of proportionality to the identity operator ($\mathbb{I}/D$) confirms the AME property.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The local dimension $d$ is the critical parameter, with existence proven for all $d \ge 3$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The classification relies on known results regarding non-existence at $d=2$ and utilizes a product property: if two states are AME, their tensor product is also AME.

**Figures summary.** Table I lists simplex codes and coset representatives; Fig. 1 illustrates the Fano plane structure on $\mathbb{Z}_7$; Table II provides certificates showing vanishing cross-terms in specific products involving shift vectors.

**Paper structure.** The paper first addresses the general problem of AME existence, then details constructions for odd dimensions ($d=q$) and dimensions congruent to $2 \pmod 4$ ($d=2^k q'$). The structure builds upon known cases (prime power dimensions) to cover all remaining $d \ge 3$ using product rules.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We prove that an absolutely maximally entangled state of seven qudits exists if and only if the local dimension satisfies $d\geq 3$. Prior to this work, to the best of our knowledge, $\text{AME}(7,d)$ states were known to exist only when $d$ is a prime power other than $2$, or when $d$ can be expressed as a product of dimensions for which existence was already known. Since it has been proved that no $\text{AME}(7,2)$ state exists, it remains to establish existence for all $d\geq 3$. We construct cyclic quadratic-phase states for every odd local dimension and develop a coupled binary--odd-dimensional construction for every dimension congruent to $2$ modulo $4$. Together with the known power-of-two cases and the product property of AME states, these constructions cover every local dimension $d\geq 3$.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously analyzes the entanglement structure of 'flower states' by computing various entanglement measures under different physical constraints, such as Local Operations and Classical Communication (LOCC) versus Non-Entangling (NE) operations. It reveals significant quantitative gaps between these resource measures, providing deep insight into how entanglement can be quantified depending on the allowed quantum manipulations. The findings establish new lower bounds for asymptotic irreversibility gaps in quantum information theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit calculation of multiple operational entanglement measures (LOCC vs. NE) for a structured class of states provides concrete benchmarks for understanding the hierarchy of quantum resources beyond standard notions like distillable entanglement.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To systematically explore the operational landscape of quantum entanglement by computing various entanglement measures for a specific class of states, revealing gaps and structural properties under different sets of allowed operations.

**Main result.** The paper establishes exact analytical expressions for multiple entanglement measures (distillable entanglement, cost under LOCC/NE) for 'flower states,' demonstrating large irreversibility gaps between these quantities.

**Method.** The analysis involves computing zero-error versions of entanglement measures using techniques related to tempered negativity and leveraging uncertainty relations over cyclic groups.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on 'flower states,' which are maximally correlated quantum states parameterized by an even local dimension $d=2k$. The results are derived for these specific, highly structured entangled states.

**Key observables.** Distillable entanglement (constant 1 ebit), Entanglement cost under LOCC ($\min_{r|k} \log(rac{r+k}{r})$), and the Irreversibility Gap ($\Delta_{NE}^{irr}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The local dimension $d=2k$, and the structure of the factorization based on divisors $r$ of $k$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on defining specific classes of states ('flower states') to achieve explicit computations for multiple entanglement measures, which is rare.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by first calculating the main entanglement measures for flower states under LOCC and NE operations. It then derives exact zero-error costs using advanced mathematical tools like tempered negativity and uncertainty principles. Finally, it analyzes structural consequences, such as the non-monotonicity of squashed entanglement.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The mysterious nature of entanglement, one of the most prominent exquisitely quantum phenomena, is reflected in its intricate operational structure, with a hierarchy of classes of free operations that enable its manipulation at different levels of effectiveness. Here we use the class of 'flower states', parametrised by their (even) local dimension $2k$, to shine light on some aspects of this varied landscape. We compute all the main entanglement measures for flower states, uncovering a large gap between all forms of distillable entanglement, equal to 1 ebit independently of the local dimension, and the entanglement cost under local operations and classical communication (LOCC), known to be equal to $\log\big(2\sqrt{k}\big)$. Even under the strictly more powerful class of non-entangling (NE) operations, we show that their cost is still equal to $\log\big(1+\sqrt{k}\big)$, only about an ebit less than for LOCCs. This result, which we prove by calculating the recently introduced tempered entanglement negativity for these states, demonstrates the largest known 'irreversibility gap', i.e. the difference between distillable entanglement and entanglement cost, under NE operations, equal to $Θ\big(\frac12 \log d\big)$, with $d$ being the local dimension. A notable consequence is that the celebrated squashed entanglement is not a monotone under NE operations. Finally, we compute the exact cost under LOCC operations for flower states; this is given by the Schmidt number, which turns out to be additive over multiple copies and equal to $\min_{r|k} \log\left( r + \frac{k}{r} \right)$; for prime $k$ this reduces to $\log(k+1)$, about twice the standard LOCC cost. These last results leverage the uncertainty relations over cyclic groups proved by Tao and Meshulam.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces the Maximum-Utility Decoder (MUD) to optimize GHZ state preparation by treating decoding as a continuous utility maximization problem rather than binary recovery. By combining MWPM with a CNN, it achieves near-optimal performance for measuring long-range quantum order in 2D lattices. This work provides a versatile framework applicable across different types of quantum error correction codes.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit connection between maximizing a continuous order parameter ($\langle\hat{M}^2angle$) in decoding algorithms bridges concepts from quantum information theory with statistical physics techniques used to analyze correlated systems (like spin glasses or disordered magnets).

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is developing an optimal decoding strategy for measurement-based GHZ state preparation that surpasses conventional methods limited to binary logical recovery.

**Main result.** The Maximum-Utility Decoder (MUD) establishes an optimal framework by maximizing the continuous expected utility ($\langle\hat{M}^2angle$), and a scalable two-stage decoder approaches near-optimal performance even in its first stage.

**Method.** The authors frame decoding as minimum Bayesian risk inference, generalizing standard decoders to use a continuous utility function. They propose a hybrid approach combining Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).

**Model / system.** The study focuses on measurement-based quantum computation protocols implemented on a two-dimensional Lieb lattice geometry, aiming to prepare macroscopic GHZ states under noise.

**Key observables.** Squared magnetization ($\langle\hat{M}^2angle$), which serves as the continuous utility function quantifying long-range order and state quality.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Noise parameters ($t_A, t_B$) defining the error model; lattice size ($N=256 	imes 256$); comparison thresholds relative to bare MWPM.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The utility function can be generalized from binary (topological) outcomes to continuous measures like magnetization for GHZ states. The two-stage decoder provides a computationally tractable approximation of the optimal solution.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the decoding process on a Lieb lattice, comparing $\langle\hat{M}^2angle$ values between MWPM and SW-MWPM, and showing decoding thresholds in parameter space.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the MUD framework by contrasting it with binary decoders. It details the physical model (Lieb lattice/RBIM), proposes the two-stage decoder (MWPM $	o$ CNN refinement), presents results comparing performance against existing methods, and discusses generalizations of the utility function.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The meticulous preparation of macroscopic Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states provides a foundational resource for quantum technologies such as metrology, cryptography, and fault-tolerant codes. While state-of-the-art measurement-based protocols offer efficient low-depth execution, their performance can be bottlenecked by conventional decoders, such as minimum weight perfect matching (MWPM) or even maximum-likelihood decoding (MLD), which optimize for $binary$ logical recovery and fail to maximize the $continuous$ long-range order characteristic of a GHZ state for two-dimensional geometries. Here we overcome this limitation by framing the decoding problem as minimum Bayesian risk inference, introducing a general paradigm that maximizes the expected ${utility}$ of the decoded state. Implementing this maximum-utility approach, we construct an algorithm that achieves the highest possible per-shot decoded quantum order and thereby establish an optimal decoding strategy for measurement-based GHZ state preparation. To improve its computational efficiency, we design a scalable two-stage decoder, which first encodes the syndromes into the edge weights of MWPM and then refines the result with a convolutional neural network trained to maximize the expected utility, at a fraction of the cost of the optimal decoder. Remarkably, we find that the first stage alone$\unicode{x2014}$which makes the matching aware of the gauge choice at no cost beyond bare MWPM$\unicode{x2014}$already performs near-optimally up to the largest sizes we study, $N=256\times256$, closing up to $87\%$ of the gap between the bare-MWPM and optimal decoding thresholds. Generalizing MWPM and MLD, the maximum-utility decoder (MUD) establishes a versatile framework that can be explicitly tailored to the operational demands of specific experiments by redefining the utility function.

</details>

**Summary.** The research analyzes single-photon emission from organic molecules operating in high optical saturation regimes, finding that standard two-level system models fail to predict observed fluorescence suppression. The authors propose and validate a model based on intensity-dependent excited-state absorption into a dark state, successfully explaining the nonlinear optical response.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides crucial experimental evidence challenging the universal applicability of simple TLS models for quantum emitters under intense driving fields, pointing toward complex nonlinear optical physics governed by matrix interactions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates deviations from the standard two-level system (TLS) description when molecular single-photon emitters are driven under strong continuous-wave optical saturation.

**Main result.** The anomalous saturation regime, characterized by fluorescence suppression and linewidth broadening, is quantitatively reproduced by a model incorporating intensity-dependent excited-state absorption into a short-lived dark state.

**Method.** The authors performed resonant and off-resonant ZPL excitation measurements across varying laser intensities, comparing observed nonlinear optical responses against theoretical predictions.

**Model / system.** The physical system is solid-state single organic molecules (e.g., DBT) embedded in nanocrystals, which are modeled using an extended quantum dynamics framework that includes intensity-dependent decay channels via Excited State Absorption (ESA).

**Key observables.** Fluorescence rate $R(I)$, ZPL linewidth $\Gamma_{	ext{zpl}}$, and the Zero-Phonon Line (ZPL) shift, all measured as functions of excitation intensity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The anomaly parameter ($\xi$), saturation intensities ($I_{	ext{res,sat}}$), and the ratio between resonant and off-resonant ESA parameters are key quantitative results.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the simple TLS model fails in the strong driving regime; the analysis rules out laser heating and intersystem crossing as the cause of the anomaly.

**Figures summary.** Figures show comparisons between standard TLS fits and observed anomalous saturation curves, alongside comparisons of temperature dependence derived from cryostat scans versus those extracted from intensity-dependent measurements.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem by observing anomalous saturation in molecular emitters; it then develops a theoretical model based on ESA into a dark state to explain the deviation; finally, it validates this model across different excitation regimes and environmental conditions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Solid-state single organic molecules, such as dibenzoterrylene (DBT) in organic matrices, are prominent deterministic single-photon sources, usually modeled as effective two-level systems (TLS). We show that single DBT molecules in anthracene nanocrystals, under strong continuous-wave driving, depart from this picture: instead of the expected saturation, fluorescence is strongly suppressed at high resonant pump power, while the linewidth broadens beyond the TLS prediction -- an \emph{anomalous saturation} regime. Comparing coherent and incoherent excitation and independently calibrating temperature via phonon-induced dephasing rules out laser-induced heating and intersystem crossing. Instead, a model of intensity-dependent excited-state absorption (ESA) toward a short-lived dark state quantitatively reproduces both the fluorescence suppression and the linewidth broadening. We further show that matrix quality mitigates this quenching, and that pulsed excitation schemes are strategic toward full population inversion, with direct implications for quantum nanophotonics and molecular optomechanics.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reinterprets ChatGPT-like AI generation not as random text prediction but as a controllable nonlinear physical system. By analyzing how output entropy changes with temperature, the authors demonstrate a phenomenon called 'population inversion.' They successfully map this behavior onto an effective dynamical equation governed by a hidden coordinate, suggesting that LLMs are fundamentally structured physical devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** It treats the complex, high-dimensional dynamics of LLMs as a physical system exhibiting phase transitions and non-equilibrium behavior, drawing direct parallels to concepts used in statistical mechanics and nonlinear physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the non-intuitive dynamics of ChatGPT-like AIs, specifically how increasing decoder temperature affects output entropy and long-term population distribution.

**Main result.** Contrary to expectation, the AI output undergoes a 'population inversion' where increased randomness leads to structured ordering rather than pure disorder. The system can be modeled by an effective nonlinear map whose hidden coordinate predicts future behavior.

**Method.** The authors analyzed 12,000 continuations across multiple AIs, classifying outputs into dynamical regimes and deriving coarse-grained variables ($m$, $S_2$) to track population shifts.

**Model / system.** The system is the autoregressive text generation process of LLMs (e.g., GPT-2, Llama), which is modeled as an iterative nonlinear physical system governed by a hidden coordinate $\mathbf{x}_n$.

**Key observables.** Output entropy ($S_2$), sign change in effective level gap ($eta_{eff}\Delta$), and the correlation coefficient ($\rho$) between the hidden coordinate's prediction and actual output repetition.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Decoder Temperature ($T_d$), which acts as a controlled physical parameter; the hidden coordinate $\mathbf{x}_n$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on coarse-graining sentences into symbols and assuming that the complex dynamics can be captured by projecting transformer operations onto a single, effective nonlinear map.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate population inversion across temperature sweeps, showing structured dynamical routes (e.g., Llama vs. Pythia) reaching an entropy maximum followed by inversion; other figures show how perturbing the hidden coordinate $\mathbf{x}_n$ predictably alters repetition rates.

**Paper structure.** The paper moves from observing counter-intuitive macroscopic behavior (population inversion with $T_d$) to developing a quantitative framework using coarse variables, and finally proposing an underlying effective nonlinear dynamical map parameterized by a measurable hidden coordinate $\mathbf{x}_n$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Increasing the temperature of an ordinary many-state system increases access to a wider range of states and hence increases its entropy. We find the opposite in ChatGPT-like AIs, even though raising the decoder temperature likewise increases access to a wider range of states (next-token choices). Across 12,000 continuations from 11 AIs, autoregressive feedback drives the long-time output population through an entropy maximum and into population inversion. The transition features frozen states, cycles, intermittency and noise-induced ordering. We present evidence of a hidden coordinate that acts as the state variable of an effective nonlinear map. Its trajectory average strongly predicts output repetition in separate test trajectories. ChatGPT-like AIs therefore behave not as `stochastic parrots', but as a new class of controllable nonlinear physical systems whose internal dynamics can be measured and perturbed.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the motion of a rotating particle in a viscoelastic fluid, finding that rotation introduces non-Markovian effects and breaks time-reversal symmetry. By developing a theoretical model based on generalized Langevin equations, the authors establish that this system serves as a minimal physical realization demonstrating Onsager–Casimir symmetry in complex stochastic dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides an accessible physical realization (colloids in viscoelastic fluids) for studying fundamental symmetries like Onsager-Casimir relations in complex, time-nonlocal stochastic dynamics, which has parallels in open quantum systems theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the stochastic dynamics of a rotating Brownian particle in a non-Markovian, viscoelastic fluid to understand how rotation breaks time-reversal symmetry beyond standard fluctuation-dissipation relations.

**Main result.** Rotation induces enhanced long-time diffusivity and generates time-antisymmetric cross-correlations, establishing the system as a minimal realization of Onsager–Casimir symmetry in time-nonlocal stochastic dynamics.

**Method.** The authors use a minimal linear model coupling the particle to a bath variable, deriving a generalized Langevin equation with a non-reciprocal memory kernel and analyzing fluctuation correlations.

**Model / system.** The system is a superparamagnetic colloidal particle rotating in a viscoelastic fluid. The dynamics are modeled using coupled Langevin equations involving an advective coupling term that breaks time-reversal symmetry.

**Key observables.** Enhanced long-time diffusivity, time-antisymmetric cross-correlations ($C_{ij}(t, t') = -C_{ij}(t', t)$), and the Magnus effect.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Rotation frequency ($\Omega$), viscoelastic fluid properties (related to memory kernel decay rates $k$ and $\gamma$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The advective coupling term is phenomenological, and the analysis relies on deriving generalized fluctuation-dissipation relations for non-Markovian noise.

**Figures summary.** Figures show schematic setups, Magnus effect trajectories, MSD vs. rotation frequency (showing enhancement), and cross-correlation components demonstrating antisymmetry.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from experimental observation of enhanced diffusion and asymmetry to developing a minimal theoretical model involving coupled Langevin equations, deriving the non-reciprocal memory kernel, and finally establishing the generalized Onsager–Casimir symmetry relation connecting correlations to transverse response.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the stochastic dynamics of a rotating Brownian particle in a non-Markovian fluid. Experimentally, we find that rotation enhances the long-time diffusivity of the particle and generates time-antisymmetric cross-correlations between orthogonal displacement components in the plane perpendicular to the rotation axis. To rationalize these observations, we introduce a minimal linear model in which a tracer is coupled to a slow bath degree of freedom and rotation enters through an advective coupling. Eliminating the bath variable yields a generalized Langevin equation with a non-reciprocal memory kernel. This kernel rotates in time, forming a logarithmic spiral, and it obeys Onsager-Casimir symmetry under reversal of the rotation vector, and the corresponding fluctuation-response relation. From the latter we obtain a geometric construction that links two-time cross-correlations to the transverse response of the particle in bulk. Unlike the ordinary Einstein relation, this relation involves the antisymmetric sector of the response. Our experiments and theory are in qualitative agreement, establishing rotating colloids in viscoelastic fluids as a minimal realization of Onsager-Casimir symmetry in time-nonlocal stochastic dynamics

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces the pseudo-quantum representation (PQR) to unify Markov chain dynamics and quantum evolution into one framework. It shows that both classical dissipation and unitary quantum mechanics emerge as specific restrictions of this single, complex-valued mathematical object. This provides a deep structural connection between statistical physics and quantum theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful mathematical bridge between classical stochastic processes and unitary quantum mechanics, suggesting that many physical systems are governed by a single underlying complex structure. This is highly relevant for open quantum systems theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to unify two seemingly distinct descriptions of dynamics—dissipative Markov chain evolution and unitary quantum evolution—by showing they both arise as restrictions of a single mathematical object: the pseudo-quantum representation (PQR).

**Main result.** The PQR generates an entire one-parameter group $Wz$, where its real slice ($z$ real) reproduces the classical Markov semigroup, and its imaginary slice ($z=i	heta$) yields a genuine unitary quantum evolution.

**Method.** The core method involves constructing the PQR using complex-orthogonal flows on a doubled state space, utilizing a bilinear pairing to achieve holomorphy in complex time $z$.

**Model / system.** The primary model is a finite, irreducible, reversible continuous-time Markov chain. The paper develops this framework by analyzing the symmetric Ehrenfest urn as a detailed example.

**Key observables.** Pseudo-density $ho_z$, pseudo-wave $\Phi_z$, Bloch vector $r$, and various divergence measures like KL divergence and Fisher–Rao distance.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The complex time parameter $z \in \mathbb{C}$, the Markov chain generator $Q$, and the clock angle $	heta(t) = \arccos(e^{-2t})$ for the Ehrenfest case.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is preliminary, focusing only on finite state spaces and the symmetric Ehrenfest urn; it also assumes standard results from Lie theory and information geometry.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds the PQR framework by defining the complex flow $Wz$, then analyzing its real slice (Markov dynamics) and imaginary slice (Quantum dynamics). It develops this using specific examples like the Ehrenfest urn, linking it to spin algebra, Lorentz boosts, and quantum circuits.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The pseudo-quantum representation re-encodes a finite, irreducible, reversible continuous-time Markov chain with $M$ states as a complex-orthogonal flow on a doubled space of dimension $2M$. After uniformisation, a square-root gauge, a doubling of the state space and a diagonal unitary twist, the chain generates an entire one-parameter group $W_z = e^{zK}$ with $z$ complex, and this single group is the object of the paper. Its real slice, $z$ real, reproduces the stochastic semigroup exactly through an explicit decoding whose probabilistic meaning is the parity of the number of ticks of the uniformised chain. Its imaginary slice, $z = iθ$, is a finite-dimensional unitary quantum system. The chain and the quantum system are therefore not two analogous models but two restrictions of one entire representation. The setup also produces, with no further input, a pseudo-Schroedinger equation, a bilinear von Neumann equation for a complex-symmetric pseudo-density, and a pseudo-Bloch vector equation on a non-compact quadric. We develop the construction from first principles and work out one model completely, the usual symmetric Ehrenfest urn. Its gauged generator equals $(2/n) J_x$, the spin-$n/2$ operator, its relaxation modes are Lorentz boosts, and its imaginary slice is a depth-one quantum circuit whose Born distribution is the classical urn law under the clock $θ(t) = \arccos(e^{-2t})$. The same clock identifies the Fisher-Rao lift of the urn trajectory with a rigid spin-coherent-state orbit. This is a preliminary simplified version of a longer paper. It treats only finite state spaces and only the symmetric Ehrenfest urn, and it previews without proofs the asymmetric urn, two queues, the symmetric simple exclusion process and the stochastic Ising model. Appendix primers make the quantum, geometric and information-theoretic language self-contained.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors demonstrate that weak far-infrared light can induce a giant insulator-to-metal transition in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene by selectively heating the electronic subsystem. This effect stems from the extreme sensitivity of the correlated many-body gap to thermal excitation, establishing MATBG as an ultra-sensitive bolometric detector for faint long-wavelength radiation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides an experimental platform demonstrating how subtle changes in electronic temperature can trigger macroscopic phase transitions (insulator-to-metal) in strongly correlated systems using low-energy photons, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum criticality and energy detection.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To investigate if weak, low-energy photons can destabilize a correlated insulator (CI) state in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) and drive it metallic, producing a giant photoresistive response.

**Main result.** The CI gap collapses upon irradiation due to electronic heating, leading to a broadband, low-noise photoresponse with high voltage responsivity. This mechanism is robust against magnetic fields and does not require structural transitions.

**Method.** Measurements involve mapping the longitudinal resistance ($R_{xx}$) under varying magnetic fields and temperature while irradiating the MATBG device with far-infrared (FIR) or millimeter-wave (MM) photons.

**Model / system.** The physical system is Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) tuned to half filling of the moiré band, which exhibits correlated insulating states at integer fillings ($
u=\pm 2$). The physics relies on the extreme sensitivity of a many-body correlated gap to weak electronic heating.

**Key observables.** Photoresistance ($R_{	ext{THz}}$), voltage responsivity (exceeding millivolts per nW), and the collapse of the correlated insulating gap ($\omega_g 	o 0$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Filling factor ($
u$), magnetic field ($B$) up to several tesla, incident photon energy comparable to the flat-band width, and electronic temperature rise ($\Delta T_e$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The photoresponse is governed purely by electronic heating suppressing the many-body gap, rather than persistent photocarrier population or lattice dynamics.

**Figures summary.** Figures show $R_{xx}$ dependence on filling and magnetic field, demonstrating CI states. Other figures map broadband photoresistance ($R_{	ext{THz}}$) vs. $
u$ and $B$, confirming the electronic origin of the response.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the CI state in MATBG, demonstrates that weak FIR/MM irradiation causes a giant resistance drop by heating the electron subsystem (CI gap collapse), quantifies this photoresponse's high sensitivity, and contrasts this mechanism with superconducting bolometers while analyzing thermalization processes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Light incident on an insulator is generally not expected to turn it into a metal without invoking intense ultrafast excitation that leads to transient structural transitions. Here we show that magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene tuned to half filling of the moiré band provides a notable exception to this expectation. We find that weak beam of long-wavelength photons, with energies comparable to the flat-band width, selectively heat the low-heat-capacity electronic subsystem, thereby suppressing the correlated gap. This produces a giant resistance change governed not by a persistent photocarrier population, but by the extreme sensitivity of a many-body correlated gap to weak electronic heating. The resulting photon-driven insulator-to-metal transition produces a broadband low-noise photoresponse with voltage responsivity exceeding millivolts per nW of absorbed power. The mechanism is dual to superconducting hot-electron response: radiation-heated electrons suppress a many-body order, but in reverse the correlated insulator melts into a metal, providing robustness to magnetic fields of several tesla and a sharp insulator-to-metal resistive contrast. Our results establish correlated flat-band systems as a platform for ultra-sensitive detection of faint long-wavelength radiation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously compares the Lindblad master equation approach with a circuit/Landauer model for calculating heat transport in quantum circuits. The authors demonstrate that while both methods agree in the weak coupling limit, they quantify the breakdown of this approximation at stronger couplings. This comparison provides crucial guidelines for applying open system dynamics theories to superconducting quantum devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it provides a rigorous cross-validation between two powerful theoretical tools (Lindblad vs. circuit theory) used to model open quantum systems, offering guidance on when approximations are valid for complex superconducting circuits.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper compares two theoretical frameworks—the Lindblad master equation approach and a circuit/Landauer model—for accurately calculating quantum heat transport mediated by thermal microwave photons in superconducting circuits.

**Main result.** For linear circuits, both models yield identical results in the weak coupling limit; however, the analysis quantifies that the weak coupling assumption limits the applicability of the Lindblad approach for quantitative predictions at larger couplings.

**Method.** The authors compare steady-state solutions derived from a Lindblad master equation (using Fermi's golden rule) against power calculations based on thermal noise spectra and transconductance in an equivalent circuit model.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as an archetypal two-bath setup where heat flows through a cavity mediating interaction between the baths. The analysis extends to include anharmonic elements like qubits, which challenge the weak coupling assumption.

**Key observables.** Heat current (P) and thermal conductance ($G_{th}$)

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coupling constants ($g_j$ or $G_{12}(\omega)$), temperature difference ($\delta T$), and the strength of coupling relative to system parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption tested is the weak coupling limit required for the Lindblad master equation approach; deviations from this limit lead to discrepancies with the circuit model.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates both the quantum Lindblad and microwave circuit approaches. Figure 3 numerically compares thermal conductance ($G_{th}$) derived from both models against varying coupling strengths, showing agreement at weak coupling but divergence otherwise.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the physical problem and details the two competing theoretical frameworks (Lindblad vs. Circuit). It then performs an analytical comparison in the linear regime, derives quantitative expressions for thermal conductance, and concludes by assessing the range of validity of the weak coupling approximation using numerical comparisons.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We compare two popular models applicable to analyzing heat transport by thermal microwave photons in quantum circuits. The first model is derived from a weak-coupling Lindblad master equation, with transition rates determined by Fermi's golden rule induced by thermal dissipation sources. The second approach employs a circuit model, where thermal Johnson-Nyquist noise generated by dissipative elements introduces currents, and consequently Joule power, in other parts of the circuit. This leads to a Landauer type expression of heat transport where the transmission coefficient is proportional to the transconductance in the circuit. We find that the two models yield identical results in a linear circuit in the weak coupling limit with an analytic expression of power in an archetypal circuit of a cavity mediating heat between two baths. Our analysis yields a quantitative assessment of the range of validity of the weak coupling assumption in a circuit. Due to the correspondence of the two results, we feel confident in applying the weak coupling Lindblad model also for analyzing heat transport in quantum circuits consisting, e.g. of qubits and/or non-linear resonators.

</details>
