**Summary.** This work demonstrates that MoSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayers can act as tunable platforms for engineering correlated electronic states like Mott insulators and Wigner crystals. By applying an out-of-plane electric field, researchers control the interlayer hybridization, showing that charge ordering is stabilized differently depending on whether the electron density is below or above one per moiré cell.

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to electrically tune correlation strength and charge ordering in a solid-state moiré system provides an accessible platform for studying fundamental many-body physics, analogous to tuning parameters in quantum simulation models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether fractional charge-ordered states, such as Generalized Wigner Crystals (GWC), can survive when interlayer hybridization is induced in moiré heterobilayers.

**Main result.** The system exhibits layer-hybridized Mott insulators and GWCs whose stability depends strongly on the electron filling factor ($n$); specifically, strong correlation is favored at fillings above one electron per moiré cell due to Coulomb repulsion overcoming tunneling.

**Method.** The research combines optical characterization (reflectance contrast spectroscopy using Rydberg excitons) with magneto-optical measurements (Magnetic Circular Dichroism, MCD) across varying out-of-plane electric fields.

**Model / system.** The physical system is an H-stacked MoSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayer. The analysis uses concepts of layer-polarized generalized Wigner crystals and Mott insulators, tunable via an external electric field that controls the band alignment between the two semiconducting layers.

**Key observables.** MCD spectra (sensitive to magnetism), doping-dependent reflectance contrast spectroscopy, hybridization energy ($t$), and charge ordering signatures at fractional fillings.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Filling factor ($n$) relative to unity, out-of-plane electric field strength ($	ext{V/nm}$), and the resulting band alignment regime (Type-I vs. Type-II).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system can be modeled by considering the competition between interlayer tunneling (kinetic energy) and on-site Coulomb repulsion, which dictates charge localization.

**Figures summary.** Figures detail doping-dependent reflectance contrast spectra showing Hubbard band splitting under varying electric fields, alongside MCD measurements confirming magnetic signatures across different hybridization regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically maps the electronic state evolution by first characterizing the moiré superlattice structure and then using electric field tuning to transition between different band alignments (Type-I $	o$ Type-II), observing changes in correlated insulating states (Mott/GWC) at varying electron fillings.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Transition metal dichalcogenide moiré heterobilayers with type-II band alignment provide a versatile platform for layer-polarized generalized Wigner crystals, in which strong Coulomb interactions drive charge ordering at fractional lattice fillings. With a finite interlayer band offset, an out-of-plane electric field can tune layer-resolved moiré bands through resonance and enable controllable interlayer hybridization. Although hybridized Mott insulators have been previously demonstrated, whether fractional charge-ordered states can survive such hybridization remains elusive. Here we drive an H-stacked MoSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayer through a type-I-to-type-II band-alignment transition and realize layer-hybridized Mott insulator and generalized Wigner crystals. For fillings below one electron per moiré cell, tunneling delocalizes electrons and modifies Wigner crystallization. However, above one electron per cell, Coulomb repulsion overcomes tunneling and favors layer-separated occupation, stabilizing stronger charge-ordered states. These results establish electrically tunable hybridized moiré heterobilayers as a powerful platform for engineering correlated charge order and exploring fractional Chern phases and emergent magnetism.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a unified theoretical framework using the time-dependent quantum geometric tensor to characterize periodically driven quantum systems. It extends concepts like Berry curvature to the time domain, deriving sum rules that link these geometric quantities directly to measurable optical responses. The findings establish this tensor as a key diagnostic tool for understanding topological and dynamical effects in Floquet matter.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides powerful diagnostic tools (the time-dependent quantum geometric tensor) for understanding how topological and geometric properties manifest in driven quantum matter, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and Floquet engineering.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is extending the concept of quantum geometry (Berry curvature and quantum metric) from static Bloch bands to periodically driven Floquet systems.

**Main result.** The authors establish a time-dependent quantum geometric tensor as a unified framework describing geometric, topological, and dynamical properties in these driven systems. They show that first-order DC Hall and longitudinal responses vanish under ideal band occupations.

**Method.** The methodology involves defining time-dependent geometric tensors in the Floquet-Bloch basis, deriving optical sum rules relating Fourier components of these tensors to measurable conductivity, and performing detailed symmetry analyses.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on two-dimensional (2D) quantum systems subjected to a time-periodic Hamiltonian, analyzed using Floquet theory. Specific models include the Rudner-Lindner-Berg-Levin (RLBL) model and fully symmetric Floquet Hamiltonians.

**Key observables.** Time-dependent Berry curvature ($\Omega_{xy}(t)$), quantum metric ($g_{xy}(t)$), optical conductivity $\sigma(\omega)$, and quantized charge pumping currents.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Periodicity $T$, quasienergy bands, harmonic frequencies $n\Omega$, and the assumption of ideal Floquet-band occupations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis heavily relies on assuming ideal occupation (bands fully filled or empty) to derive zero DC response sum rules. It also assumes orthogonality for the Floquet states.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate time dependence of phase band extrema, components of geometric tensors ($G_{xy}^-, G_{xt}^-$), and confirm analytical predictions regarding conductivity zeros and sum rules.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the time-dependent quantum geometric tensor in Floquet systems to deriving optical sum rules. It then explores non-adiabatic charge pumping via mixed Berry curvature, followed by a comprehensive symmetry analysis constraining the tensor components.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The quantum geometry of Bloch bands, characterized by the Berry curvature and the quantum metric, underpins a wide range of linear and nonlinear responses in static systems. Here, we extend this framework to periodically driven (Floquet) systems by introducing a time-dependent Berry curvature and quantum metric defined directly in the Floquet-Bloch basis. We derive optical sum rules that relate the Fourier components of these geometric quantities to the optical conductivity and demonstrate that, under ideal Floquet-band occupations, the first-order DC Hall and longitudinal responses at harmonic frequencies vanish identically. We further introduce a mixed Berry curvature involving time and momentum derivatives, which gives rise to a non-adiabatic quantized charge-pumping mechanism that occurs naturally during each driving period without requiring adiabatic evolution. In addition, we identify the time-domain quantum metric as a measure of the energy fluctuations of a Floquet band and interpret its mixed components as quantifying polarization-energy correlations. A comprehensive symmetry analysis reveals how time-reversal, sublattice (chiral), particle-hole, inversion, rotational, and reflection symmetries constrain the time-dependent quantum geometric tensor and its associated topological invariant. Numerical simulations of the Rudner-Lindner-Berg-Levin model and a fully symmetric Floquet model confirm the analytical predictions. These results establish the time-dependent quantum geometric tensor as a unified framework for describing the geometric, topological, and dynamical properties of periodically driven quantum systems, with direct implications for optical spectroscopy, quantum transport, and topological charge-pumping experiments.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates traveling shock fronts in a lossy nonlinear transmission line by solving an inverse problem for the required voltage-charge relation. The authors derive both exact and approximate solutions, demonstrating that physical constraints select a shock front. The work rigorously distinguishes between shocks and kinks using characteristic analysis of the underlying partial differential equations.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly quantum mechanical, the mathematical techniques used—solving nonlinear PDEs, inverse problem formulation, and analyzing wave front structures (shocks/kinks)—are highly relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in open quantum systems or classical field theories derived from quantum models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper solves an inverse problem to determine the voltage-charge relation required for a specific hyperbolic-tangent traveling front profile in a lossy nonlinear transmission line.

**Main result.** Both exact and approximate constructions confirm that physical admissibility selects a shock front, and the results show asymptotic agreement up to order m^-2 in the broad-front limit.

**Method.** The authors employed an inverse problem approach by prescribing the $	anh$ profile, alongside constructing an approximation assuming a cubic voltage-charge relation and using characteristic analysis on the underlying PDEs.

**Model / system.** The system is a lossy nonlinear transmission line modeled by coupled partial differential equations. The dynamics are reduced to an ODE for traveling waves, characterized by nonlinearity and damping terms.

**Key observables.** Normalized force $eF(v)$, the distinction between compressive shocks (Lax-type) and noncompressive kinks via characteristic analysis, and the voltage-charge relation expressed using the Gauss hypergeometric function.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Dimensionless width parameter ($m$), dimensionless squared wave speed ($w$), and the front velocity $U$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The exact solution is found by prescribing a $	anh$ profile. The approximation assumes a cubic voltage-charge relation, and the analysis relies on continuum approximations of discrete unit cells.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the exact normalized force $eF(v)$ with the least-squares approximation $e_{FG}(v)$ across various parameters ($m$ and $w$), illustrating asymptotic agreement.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by setting up the PDE model, solving the inverse problem exactly to find the required voltage-charge relation (involving ${}_2F_1$), developing an approximate solution via cubic fitting, and finally using characteristic analysis to rigorously distinguish between shock and kink solutions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate traveling fronts in a lossy nonlinear transmission line. By prescribing a hyperbolic-tangent profile with dimensionless width $m$, we solve the inverse problem of determining the voltage--charge relation for which this profile is an exact solution. The exact relation is expressed in terms of the Gauss hypergeometric function. We also construct an approximate solution by assuming a cubic voltage--charge relation and replacing the resulting quadratic damping function with its optimal linear least-squares approximation. This construction determines the cubic coefficients and yields a modified governing equation that admits the prescribed profile as an exact solution. In both constructions, physical admissibility selects a shock front. In the broad-front limit, the approximate normalized force agrees with the exact result through order $m^{-2}$; numerical comparisons show that the agreement remains good even outside the asymptotic region of large $m$. Finally, a characteristic analysis of the original partial differential equations distinguishes compressive shocks from noncompressive kinks without recourse to the mechanical analogy.

</details>

**Summary.** This research experimentally and theoretically examines exciton emission dynamics in semiconductor QDs embedded in NWs. By combining time-resolved photoluminescence with advanced simulations, the authors quantify how QD size, composition, and the surrounding waveguide structure modulate the radiative lifetime via the Purcell effect. This provides critical guidelines for engineering solid-state quantum light sources for telecom applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses open quantum systems by quantifying how engineered photonic environments (waveguides) modify fundamental quantum decay rates, a key concept in solid-state quantum emitters for quantum information.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how quantum dot (QD) emission dynamics, specifically exciton lifetime, are influenced by the QD size, composition, and the surrounding nanowire (NW) geometry.

**Main result.** The radiative lifetime is strongly dependent on the photonic environment; thin NW shells can cause significant spontaneous emission inhibition via the Purcell effect, while structural changes influence the intrinsic QD potential.

**Method.** A combination of time-resolved photoluminescence measurements and advanced theoretical modeling, including 8-band k.p calculations, configuration-interaction models, and FDTD simulations for optical confinement, was employed.

**Model / system.** The system involves zincblende InAsxP1-x QDs embedded within InP nanowires grown via CBE. The analysis considers the interplay between material properties (composition/size) and the photonic environment provided by the NW waveguide structure.

**Key observables.** Exciton lifetime ($	au$), Purcell factor ($F_P$), emission wavelength, and spectral dependence of these quantities.

**Important parameters / regimes.** QD composition ($x$), QD height, InP shell thickness (e.g., 55 nm vs 150 nm), and the resulting optical confinement modes ($	ext{HE}_{11}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis requires considering both changes in the intrinsic QD potential and the external photonic environment (Purcell effect) for a full understanding.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate PL spectra, measured decay times across different sample geometries (A, B, C), and calculated Purcell factors ($F_p$) as a function of emission wavelength.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows an experimental/theoretical cycle: structural characterization ($	ext{STEM}$/$	ext{EDS}$) informs the theoretical models ($\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p}$, CI) which are then used to interpret time-resolved PL measurements across varying NW geometries and QD parameters.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hereby, we present an experimental and theoretical investigation of emission dynamics in zincblende InAsxP1-x quantum dots (QDs) embedded in InP nanowires (NWs) grown via vapour-liquid-solid mechanism by chemical beam epitaxy, using Au nanoparticles as a nucleation catalyst. By measuring time-resolved photoluminescence from an ensemble of QD-NWs it was possible to determine the exciton lifetime dependence on QD composition and height. Changes in the InP shell thickness surrounding the InP NW stem with a QD, brought additional insight into the influence of photonic environment on the carrier dynamics. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, provided actual structural parameters. The experimentally obtained lifetimes were interpreted in the light of results of 8 band kp calculations combined with configuration-interaction model to take into account the Coulomb interactions and finite-difference time domain photonic simulations to include the effect of optical confinement. The full understanding of the experimental results required considering both, the changes in the QD potential and the Purcell effect, the latter leading to spontaneous emission inhibition in the case of NWs with thin InP shell.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the transmission of magnetic skyrmions across various planar interfaces (e.g., FM/AFM). Using micromagnetic simulations, the authors demonstrate that these interfaces function as active transport elements whose behavior is dictated by the specific magnetic order change. The results provide reduced design criteria for engineering functional spintronic devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on magnetism, the concept of 'active transport' across engineered boundaries, governed by local field equations and energy minimization principles, shares conceptual links with open quantum systems dynamics where boundary conditions dictate system evolution.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how chiral spin textures, specifically skyrmions, maintain their structural integrity when driven across abrupt material interfaces with varying magnetic order.

**Main result.** Planar interfaces act as active transport elements, and the transmission outcome (e.g., compact vs. deformed) depends critically on the interface type (FM-FM, FM-AFM, etc.) and underlying material parameters.

**Method.** The research employs continuum micromagnetic simulations combined with analytic reduced-coordinate criteria to map out phase diagrams for skyrmion transmission.

**Model / system.** The system is an ultrathin film modeled by the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation, considering four types of planar interfaces (FM-FM, AFM-AFM, FM-AFM, AFM-FM). The energy functional includes bulk terms and explicit interface coupling energies.

**Key observables.** Skyrmion transmission outcome classified as compact transmission, deformed skyrmions, stripe-domain states, amorphous textures, or relaxation into the background.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Reduced Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI), effective anisotropy, and dimensionless chirality ratios ($\kappa$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The material parameters are assumed to be piecewise constant across the interface; the model uses micromagnetic approximations for texture dynamics.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the general source-receiving geometry and provides block representations for the four studied planar interface classes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically develops the governing equations (LLG, energy functional) for different interface types, derives specific boundary conditions at the interface ($\Gamma$), analyzes the resulting phase diagrams using reduced parameters, and concludes by classifying interfaces as active transport elements.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Lateral magnetic interfaces provide a direct way to test whether skyrmions remain robust when driven across abrupt changes in material parameters and magnetic order. Here we study skyrmion transmission across planar ferromagnet-ferromagnet (FM-FM), antiferromagnet-antiferromagnet (AFM-AFM), ferromagnet-antiferromagnet (FM-AFM), and antiferromagnet-ferromagnet (AFM-FM) interfaces using micromagnetic simulations and analytic reduced-coordinate criteria. The outcomes are organized into phase diagrams according to the morphology formed in the receiving region, distinguishing compact transmission from deformed skyrmions, stripe-domain states, amorphous textures, and relaxation into the background. Same-order FM-FM and AFM-AFM skyrmion transmission is captured by an analytically defined range of the reduced Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, identifying the wall-softening regime that supports compact transmission without stripe formation. Mixed-order FM-AFM and AFM-FM interfaces are directionally distinct, requiring conversion between ferromagnetic magnetization and antiferromagnetic Néel textures. These results show that planar interfaces act as active transport elements and provide reduced design criteria for heterogeneous skyrmion tracks.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes electron localization in lattices subjected to an electric field via the Wannier-Stark potential. It mathematically derives that these states are localized (Bessel functions), leading to insulating bulk behavior. By extending the model to 2D, it demonstrates how this confinement can create distinct metallic edge states alongside an insulating interior.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, solvable model for how external fields can induce topological or boundary phenomena in condensed matter systems, which is highly relevant for understanding engineered quantum materials and interfaces.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates Wannier-Stark localization, confinement, and the resulting edge states that appear at the boundary between a bulk material and vacuum when subjected to an electric field.

**Main result.** In 1D, the system is always insulating due to localized Wannier-Stark states; however, extending to 2D allows for the construction of models exhibiting both an insulating bulk and potentially metallic edge states.

**Method.** The analysis relies on solving tight-binding Hamiltonians in the presence of a linear potential, leading to eigenfunctions expressible in terms of Bessel functions.

**Model / system.** The model is non-interacting electrons on a 2D lattice subjected to a Wannier-Stark potential generated by an electric field along one axis. The physics transitions from 1D chains (analyzed via recurrence relations) to 2D lattices with transverse tunneling.

**Key observables.** Localization length ($\xi$), electron occupation profile $n(j;x)$, and the energy spectrum showing discrete Wannier-Stark levels coupled to continuous transverse bands.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimensionless parameter $x = 2t/(eaF)$ controls the degree of localization, with limits analyzed for large ($x 	o \infty$) and small ($x 	o 0$) electric fields.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Initially assumes non-interacting electrons; later incorporates electron-electron interactions (Hubbard/nearest-neighbor) to study correlated effects near the edge.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the localization of states in 1D, the occupation profile decaying across an edge region at half-filling, and the resulting energy band structure in 2D.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the 1D Wannier-Stark ladder using Bessel functions to analyzing the many-electron filling (insulating bulk) before extending the formalism to a 2D lattice model that reveals metallic edge possibilities.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The boundary between a system's bulk and the vacuum can be modeled by a potential which confines the electrons to the bulk. Here we present the example of the Wannier-Stark linear potential, generated by an electric field along one axis of a two-dimensional lattice. Along that axis, the potential generates electronic states which are localized around each lattice site, with eigenenergies which form the Wannier-Stark ladder. In the transverse direction, the states are governed by a tight binding model with free Bloch states. In the ground state, filling these states under the Pauli principle generates an insulating bulk and an edge which can be metallic in the transverse direction. This paper explains the concepts of localization, localization length, filling and confinement. The paper also acquaints the readers with the use of Bessel functions in the solution of a simple physical model. These topics can be easily included in courses on solid state physics, and only require prior knowledge of quantum mechanics.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel Floquet spin-group framework that unifies the study of light-induced spin splitting in collinear magnets. By combining crystal symmetry with the dynamical symmetry of polarized light, the authors provide systematic rules for engineering specific types of electronic band structures. This allows researchers to precisely control magnetic properties by tailoring external optical driving fields.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful theoretical tool—a symmetry classification scheme—to predict and engineer electronic properties in magnetic materials using external electromagnetic fields, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems research.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is establishing a unified symmetry principle connecting the dynamical symmetry of incident light to the resulting spin-split electronic band structures in magnetic materials.

**Main result.** The authors developed a Floquet spin-group framework that systematically classifies allowed parity and momentum dependence for light-induced spin splittings, enabling the switching between different splitting types (odd, even, mixed) using tailored driving fields.

**Method.** The methodology combines crystal spin point group theory with the dynamical symmetry group of light to define a governing Floquet spin group ($\mathcal{G}_D$). This framework is applied via time-dependent Hamiltonian analysis and quasienergy constraints.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on collinear magnets, particularly altermagnets (AM) and antiferromagnets (AFM), modeled with negligible spin-orbit coupling. The system dynamics are governed by a Floquet Hamiltonian derived from periodic driving by light fields (CPL or BLPL).

**Key observables.** Spin-resolved quasienergy bands, the parity of spin splitting (odd/even/mixed), and higher-order wave splittings ($h$-wave, $k$-wave).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The driving field parameters, such as polarization type (CPL vs. BLPL) and relative phases ($\alpha$), act as crucial tuning knobs.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework is initially developed for collinear magnets with negligible spin-orbit coupling, although it claims general applicability.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the generators defining the dynamical light group ($	ilde{G}_L$) and provide schematic classification tables showing how different light symmetries dictate the resulting parity of spin splittings in AMs.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem by noting the lack of a unified symmetry principle. It then develops the Floquet spin-group framework, applies it to classify various splitting types (2D and 3D), and concludes with specific examples demonstrating how light polarization controls these symmetries.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Altermagnets combine momentum-dependent spin splitting with vanishing net magnetization, opening new opportunities for spintronics. Recent studies have shown that periodic driving by linearly or circularly polarized light, as well as by multicolor light fields, can control spin splitting in altermagnets and conventional antiferromagnets, and can even generate spin splitting patterns absent in equilibrium. Despite this progress, a unified principle connecting the dynamical symmetry of light to the symmetry of spin-split bands remains lacking, limiting the systematic design of light-induced spin structures. Here, by combining the spin group of crystals with the dynamical group of light, we establish a unified Floquet spin group framework for the study of periodically driven collinear magnets with negligible spin-orbit coupling. This framework systematically determines the allowed parity, momentum dependence, and nodal structure of spin splitting under different driving protocols. Guided by this symmetry classification, we show that odd-parity, even-parity, and mixed-parity spin splittings can be switched within the same material by tailoring the driving field. We further uncover higher-order $h$-wave and $k$-wave spin splittings in three-dimensional systems. Our work establishes a unified symmetry framework for light-controlled spin splitting and provides general principles for engineering nonequilibrium spin-band structures in altermagnets and related magnetic materials.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on achieving 'vibrational ladder climbing'—the stepwise excitation to high vibrational states—in CO/Pt(111) using tip-enhanced sum-frequency generation (TE-SFG). By coupling near-field plasmonics with ultrafast spectroscopy, the authors demonstrate a powerful technique for non-equilibrium control over molecular vibrations. This opens a promising pathway for manipulating chemical reactions by precisely controlling vibrational energy at the nanoscale.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of quantum control at the nanoscale. Using TE-SFG allows for probing ultrafast, non-equilibrium vibrational dynamics in surface molecules, which is a core topic in AMO physics and quantum optics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to actively control molecular reactions by accessing high-lying vibrational energy states, which are difficult to reach using conventional methods.

**Main result.** The study successfully demonstrated the stepwise population of higher vibrational levels (vibrational ladder climbing) in CO adsorbed on Pt(111) using tip-enhanced sum-frequency generation (TE-SFG).

**Method.** The research combines ultrafast, time-resolved TE-SFG spectroscopy with numerical simulations based on solving the optical Bloch equations.

**Model / system.** The system involves CO molecules adsorbed on a Pt(111) surface, probed within the near-field nanogap of an STM tip. The dynamics are modeled using anharmonic potentials (Morse potential) and solved via the optical Bloch equations.

**Key observables.** Sequential appearance of 'hot-band peaks' corresponding to transitions like $0ightarrow 1$, $1ightarrow 2$, up to $3ightarrow 4$; these hot bands are non-thermal and decay rapidly in time delay ($	au=5 	ext{ ps}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The process is highly dependent on the near-field enhancement provided by the plasmonic tip gap, with simulations showing field enhancements up to $10^6$. The accessible vibrational level is limited by the IR excitation bandwidth.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Key assumptions include that the observed hot bands are due to intra-pulse excitation rather than population accumulation over successive pulses. Model limitations include neglecting intermolecular dipole–dipole coupling and instantaneous frequency shifts.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematics of the TE-SFG setup, show the sequential appearance of multiple resonant peaks as IR pulse energy increases, and compare experimental spectra with simulations based on time evolution calculations.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the need for high vibrational state control, details the use of TE-SFG in the STM nanogap to overcome limitations, presents evidence of stepwise population transfer (VLC), validates this using theoretical models (optical Bloch equations), and concludes by discussing the bandwidth limitation on excitation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Achieving high-lying vibrational states is essential for actively controlling molecular reactions. We demonstrate vibrational ladder climbing of CO adsorbed on Pt(111) within the plasmonic tip-substrate nanogap formed in a scanning tunneling microscope, detected via tip-enhanced sum-frequency generation (TE-SFG). As the infrared pulse energy increases, hot-band peaks appear sequentially up to the 3-4 transition, indicating the stepwise population of higher vibrational states. Numerical analysis using the optical Bloch equations captures the observed energy dependence of these features. These results demonstrate the capability of TE-SFG to probe vibrational ladder climbing in surface molecular systems and suggest a promising route toward accessing high-lying vibrational states and controlling vibrational excitation at the nanoscale.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically analyzes how a single excitation moves coherently within a finite segment of a biomolecular chain. It shows that the migration dynamics are dominated by complex quantum interference patterns rather than simple classical diffusion. Crucially, it reveals that boundary conditions and the initial placement of the excitation induce measurable asymmetries in the probability distribution.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed quantum mechanical description of energy transport in nanoscale biological systems, bridging concepts from polaron physics and quantum walks to explain non-trivial spatial localization effects governed by geometry.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the coherent migration of a single excitation injected into a finite segment of a biomolecular chain.

**Main result.** The probability distribution exhibits an asymmetry for symmetrically placed nodes, which is solely due to the initial asymmetric placement within the finite boundary. The dynamics are governed by quantum interference rather than classical propagation.

**Method.** The analysis involves solving time-dependent equations of motion derived from a modified Holstein model using techniques like Laplace transforms and relating the problem to continuous-time quantum walk models.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as a finite molecular segment (MS) within a biomolecular chain, described by an adapted Holstein Hamiltonian coupling electronic excitations to lattice vibrations. The excitation forms a self-trapped state resembling a nonadiabatic polaron.

**Key observables.** Time-dependent probability distribution of the excitation at nodes ($p_n(t)$), asymmetry in this distribution, and interference patterns.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The initial excitation position ($n_0$), boundary conditions (finite length $K$), and dimensionless parameters related to coupling strength ($S$) and hopping ($B$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes the excitation cannot leave the finite segment, employs a Lang-Firsov unitary transformation, and uses a mean-field approximation that neglects incoherent polaron–phonon scattering.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Time-Probability Spectrum (TPS) showing deviations from symmetry at later times due to boundary effects, and demonstrate how the probability distribution evolves based on whether the initial excitation site is central or off-center.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical model using a modified Holstein Hamiltonian; it then applies polaron transformations and mean-field approximations to derive equations of motion for the correlation functions. The core analysis focuses on solving these equations to determine the time evolution, highlighting geometric effects like boundary asymmetry.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the migration of a single excitation excited at a structural element of a finite molecular segment, which is a part of a long biomolecular chain. The excitation cannot leave the segment and is locally coupled to thermal vibrations of the lattice, forming a self-trapped state corresponding to a nonadiabatic polaron. The time-dependent probability distribution of finding the excitation at the nodes of the segment is calculated, with particular emphasis on the role of the initial excitation position. A formal analogy is observed between the present model and continuous-time quantum walk models on finite chains with reflecting boundaries. The results reveal an asymmetry in the probability distribution for nodes symmetrically positioned with respect to the initially excited site, which arises solely from the asymmetric placement of the initial excitation within the finite segment. The only exception occurs when the initially excited node is located at the center of the segment, where the probability distribution becomes symmetric. The complex interference pattern and the absence of well-defined revivals stem from the non-equidistant spectrum of mode frequencies, leading to progressive dephasing of the constituent modes. As a result, the initially well-localized probability maximum fragments into one dominant maximum accompanied by several secondary maxima of lower intensity. These findings highlight the importance of boundary conditions and initial-state geometry in controlling quantum transport in finite molecular systems.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors experimentally investigate how the Superconducting Diode Effect (SDE) behaves in bilayer graphene SQUIDs when driven by microwaves at high frequencies. They demonstrate that the diode efficiency deviates significantly from predictions based on low-frequency adiabatic theory, showing complex power dependencies and oscillations. This work establishes BLG SQUIDs as a versatile platform for studying dynamic superconducting junction properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work explores non-linear, time-dependent quantum electrodynamics effects in superconducting circuits. The transition from adiabatic to non-adiabatic regimes provides a rich testing ground for generalized Josephson junction models beyond simple DC approximations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the microwave response of the Superconducting Diode Effect (SDE) in superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) beyond the simple adiabatic driving regime.

**Main result.** At high microwave frequencies, the diode efficiency exhibits non-monotonic power dependence, sign reversal, and oscillatory characteristics, which are successfully modeled using the resistively shunted junction model with extracted current-phase relations.

**Method.** The research combines DC transport measurements of $V$-$I$ curves and differential resistance ($dI/dV$) with microwave irradiation experiments across various frequencies. Theoretical analysis involves fitting the Josephson junction Current-Phase Relationship (CPR) using harmonic expansions.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a SQUID built from proximitized bilayer graphene, featuring superconducting Josephson junctions. The system dynamics are modeled using the Resistively Shunted Junction (RSJ) model and analyzed via time-dependent simulations incorporating extracted CPRs.

**Key observables.** Diode efficiency ($\eta$), switching currents ($I_{sw}^\pm$), Shapiro steps, and the dependence of $\eta$ on microwave power ($P$) and driving frequency ($f$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Microwave frequencies (e.g., 1.2 GHz up to 10.8 GHz), magnetic flux ($\Phi/\Phi_0$), and microwave power ($P$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often relies on fitting the CPR using a truncated harmonic series, and simulations are sometimes restricted to low-power regimes to avoid heating effects.

**Figures summary.** Figures show $V$-$I$ characteristics demonstrating SDE modulated by magnetic flux; subsequent figures map out $\eta$ vs. microwave power at various frequencies, revealing deviations from simple monotonic behavior.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from basic characterization of the SDE in BLG SQUIDs under DC bias and low-frequency microwaves (adiabatic regime) to detailed analysis of high-frequency responses, culminating in fitting CPRs and simulating the frequency-dependent power response of $\eta$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Microwave irradiation has emerged as a promising means to tune the superconducting diode effect (SDE) in Josephson junction devices. Previous experimental studies have mainly focused on the adiabatic-driving regime, in which the diode efficiency increases monotonically with microwave power and can approach the ideal value of unity. Beyond this regime, however, the microwave response of the SDE remains largely unexplored experimentally. In this work, we investigate the microwave response of the SDE in bilayer-graphene-based superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) under a broad range of driving frequencies. We show that increasing the driving frequency changes the response characteristics of the diode efficiency to microwave power--the dependence of the diode efficiency evolves from monotonic enhancement with increasing microwave power in the adiabatic regime to non-monotonic behavior beyond this regime, and ultimately to sign-reversal as well oscillatory characteristics at sufficiently high frequencies. We find that these experimentally observed frequency-dependent power response characteristics of the diode efficiency can be qualitatively captured by simulations based on the resistively shunted junction model using the device current-phase relations extracted from the experiments. These results establish SQUIDs made from bilayer graphene as a versatile platform for studying dynamic properties of superconducting junction devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports on the anisotropic transport of Josephson vortices in atomic-layer superconducting films grown on vicinal surfaces. By combining STM imaging with detailed magneto-transport measurements, the authors demonstrate that vortex motion is highly directionally dependent, exhibiting regimes ranging from thermally activated creep to quantum tunneling. The findings map out a complex phase diagram governed by the underlying atomic step structure.

**Why it may be interesting.** The strong structural control (atomic steps) leading to highly anisotropic quantum dynamics provides an excellent platform for studying dimensionality crossover, pinning mechanisms, and non-equilibrium transport phenomena in superconductors.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how Josephson vortices, formed at atomic steps on superconducting surfaces, exhibit highly anisotropic transport properties.

**Main result.** The vortex transport shows extreme anisotropy ($\sim 10^3$), leading to distinct regimes of motion—from thermally activated creep to one-dimensional pinning-free flow and quantum tunneling—all dependent on the direction relative to the atomic steps.

**Method.** Magneto-transport measurements (sheet resistance vs. T and B) are combined with Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) to visualize vortex cores and map out the phase diagram.

**Model / system.** The system is an atomic-layer superconductor, Si(111)-($\sqrt{7}	imes\sqrt{3}$)-In, grown on a vicinal surface featuring distinct atomic steps. Josephson vortices are hypothesized to dominate transport at these structural features.

**Key observables.** Sheet resistance ($R_{	ext{sheet}}$), vortex mobility ($\mu_\phi$), activation energy ($U_{	ext{act}}$), and the anisotropy ratio $\alpha$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature (0.4 to 4.2 K), out-of-plane magnetic field (B), and the relative orientation of current/Lorentz force with respect to atomic steps.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The transport phenomena are dominated by Josephson vortices localized at the atomic steps, which act as effective Josephson junctions.

**Figures summary.** Figures show STM topography confirming step structures and ZBC images visualizing elongated bright regions identified as Josephson vortex cores. Transport data map out $R_{	ext{sheet}}$ vs. T and B, revealing anisotropic behavior.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical system via STM characterization, then presents transport measurements comparing current parallel versus perpendicular to steps. The analysis quantifies the anisotropy in mobility and maps out a complex B-T phase diagram detailing different vortex flow regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Atomic steps have strong influences on surface two-dimensional superconductors. Josephson vortices formed at the atomic steps under magnetic fields may dominate transport phenomena at low temperatures, but its experimental verification is still lacking. Here, we report the vortex transport properties of atomic-layer superconductor Si(111)-$(\sqrt{7}\times\sqrt{3})$-In with vicinal surfaces, for which Josephson vortices are directly observed by scanning tunneling microscopy. A sharp drop in resistance with decreasing temperature $T$, detected under out-of-plane magnetic field $B$, reveals a distinctive anisotropy with respect to the atomic step direction. The anisotropy of sheet resistance, proportional to that of vortex mobility, amounts to the order of $10^3$ at intermediate magnetic fields. In the high-$T$ and low-$B$ region, Josephson vortices exhibit thermally excited creep motions with anisotropic activation energy $U_\mathrm{act}$. A further increase in $B$ suppresses $U_\mathrm{act}$ toward zero anisotropically, resulting in one-dimensional pinning-free vortex flow at $0.10 \lesssim B \lesssim 0.20$ T. At the lowest temperatures, the vortex motion is governed by quantum tunneling. A $B$-$T$ phase diagram constructed based on these measurements reveals multiple regions characterized by directionally dependent vortex-transport mechanisms.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically investigates the Spin Josephson Diode Effect (SJDE) in a diffusive junction containing Rashba metal. By deriving expressions for both first- and second-harmonic spin currents, the authors demonstrate that the SJDE can be achieved intrinsically via an emergent $\phi_0$ phase shift, eliminating the need for external magnetic fields or structural asymmetries.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical mechanism for non-reciprocal transport in superconducting junctions driven purely by internal material symmetries (RSOI/exchange field), which is highly relevant to understanding spin-charge conversion phenomena in mesoscopic devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the mechanism behind the Spin Josephson Diode Effect (SJDE) in a diffusive Josephson junction, aiming to show how non-reciprocal spin transport can occur without external magnetic fields.

**Main result.** The SJDE is shown to arise from the interplay between first- and second-harmonic spin Josephson currents, which generate an intrinsic $\phi_0$ phase shift due to Rashba spin-orbit coupling (RSOI) and a ferromagnetic exchange field.

**Method.** The theoretical analysis employs the quasiclassical Green's function framework to derive analytical expressions for both the first- and second-harmonic spin Josephson currents.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a diffusive Josephson junction structure incorporating a Rashba metal layer sandwiched between superconducting and ferromagnetic barriers (S/FF/F/RM/F/S).

**Key observables.** Spin Josephson Currents (FHSJC and SHSJC), the intrinsic $\phi_0$ phase shift, and the SJDE efficiency ($\eta_s$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Rashba spin-orbit interaction strength ($\alpha_R$), junction thickness ($d_m$), and temperature ($T$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis uses a perturbative expansion near $T_c$ and assumes the thick ferromagnetic layer acts as a barrier suppressing spin-singlet pairs.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the S/FL/F/RM/FR/S junction structure, while derived equations present the functional forms for the harmonic currents.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by establishing the physical necessity of breaking $P$ and $T$ symmetries, deriving analytical expressions for both first- and second-harmonic spin Josephson currents using Green's functions, and finally analyzing how the interplay between these harmonics generates the intrinsic SJDE.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We theoretically investigate the spin Josephson diode effect (SJDE) in a diffusive Josephson junction with a Rashba metal layer under a ferromagnetic exchange field. Within the quasiclassical Green's function framework, we derive analytical expressions for the first- and second-harmonic spin Josephson currents. The interplay between Rashba spin-orbit interaction and the exchange field breaks inversion and time-reversal symmetries, generating additional cosine terms in the spin current-phase relations and a finite phi0 phase shift. This phase shift induces an intrinsic asymmetry between forward and backward spin currents, leading to the SJDE without an external magnetic field. Numerical results show that the efficiency decreases with increasing metal thickness due to suppression of the second-harmonic component, while its dependence on spin-orbit interaction strength reflects competing effects between phase shift enhancement and harmonic suppression. These findings demonstrate that the interplay between harmonic components provides a mechanism for nonreciprocal spin transport without requiring suppression of spin-singlet correlations.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically analyzes pure spin currents in the surface states of topological insulators, focusing on the role of hexagonal warping. By extending linear response theory to the second order, the authors predict the existence of measurable intrinsic and extrinsic in-plane spin currents. This work is significant for spintronics as it provides a detailed understanding of non-linear spin transport mechanisms governed by crystal symmetry.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for understanding higher-order transport phenomena in topological materials, which is crucial for designing next-generation spintronic devices that rely on non-linear spin manipulation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work investigates both linear and non-linear pure spin currents generated in the surface states of topological insulators (TIs). It specifically addresses how hexagonal warping influences these transport phenomena.

**Main result.** The second-order response yields measurable intrinsic and extrinsic in-plane spin currents, which are distinct from the purely out-of-plane current found in linear response. The crystal symmetry dictates that only specific components of the spin conductivity tensor survive.

**Method.** The authors extend conserved spin transport formalism to the non-linear regime by using perturbation theory on Bloch states and solving the Boltzmann transport equation for the non-equilibrium distribution function.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled using the surface states of 3D TIs like Bi2Te3, incorporating an effective low-energy Hamiltonian that includes a hexagonal warping term. This warping provides a well-defined Berry curvature while preserving time-reversal symmetry.

**Key observables.** Pure spin current (both linear and second-order), Spin Hall Effect components ($\Xi^l_{ab}$), Intrinsic and Extrinsic Second-Order Spin Conductivity (SOSC) components ($\Gamma^l_{	ext{int}}, \Gamma^l_{	ext{ext}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Hexagonal warping strength ($\lambda$), Fermi energy ($E_F$ or $k_F$), and the relaxation time approximation ($	au$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on extending the formalism to second-order in the electric field, using perturbation theory for eigenstates, and employing the relaxation time approximation in the Boltzmann equation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate Fermi contours showing hexagonal warping distortion, momentum space distributions of Berry curvature and SOSC components, and plots detailing how spin conductivity varies with Fermi energy.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the linear response (purely out-of-plane current) to motivating the non-linear extension. It then derives second-order terms involving BCP and BC dipoles, calculates the total spin current via the Boltzmann equation, and finally analyzes the symmetry constraints imposed by the material's crystal structure.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Spin Hall effect is one of the primary sources of pure spin current in spintronic devices, observed in spin-orbit coupled materials. In this work, we investigate linear and non-linear pure spin currents in the hexagonally warped surface states of topological insulators like $\rm Bi_2Te_3$, using the formalism of conserved spin transport. The hexagonal warping effect enables the application of this formalism by providing a well-defined Berry curvature without breaking the time-reversal symmetry. The absence of in-plane spin currents in the linear response motivates the extension of the formalism to the non-linear regime, by combining the perturbation of Bloch states with the Boltzmann transport equation. The second-order response exhibits both intrinsic and extrinsic in-plane spin currents induced by the spin-weighted Berry curvature, Berry connection polarizability (BCP) dipole and Berry curvature dipole (BCD) respectively. The band anisotropy due to the $C_{3v}$ symmetry of the material ($\rm Bi_2Te_3$) propagates through the spin textures and the band geometric quantities, resulting in the selection of certain components of the spin conductivity tensors.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically examines how coupling a TMD monolayer to a chiral antiferromagnet alters its electronic and optical behavior. Using an effective $k\cdot p$ model, the authors predict measurable effects like the Anomalous Hall Effect and exciton resonance splitting. These predictions allow for potential experimental detection via magneto-optical measurements of the magnetization orientation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work connects magnetism, topology (Berry curvature), and low-dimensional materials physics, providing theoretical tools for understanding emergent quantum phenomena in hybrid systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how proximity effects from a chiral $120^\circ$ Néel magnetic structure modify the transport and optical properties of Transition Metal Dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers.

**Main result.** The proximity effect induces an Anomalous Antiferromagnetic Hall Effect (AHE) and causes splitting/mixing of exciton resonances, even in the absence of net magnetization.

**Method.** The authors developed an effective $k\cdot p$ model derived from a six-band tight binding approach to calculate transport coefficients and optical transition matrix elements.

**Model / system.** The system is a TMD ML coupled to a chiral magnet, modeled using an effective Hamiltonian that incorporates exchange interaction, spin-orbit coupling, and symmetry-breaking terms. The analysis focuses on the electronic structure near $K_{\pm}$ and $\Gamma$ points.

**Key observables.** Anomalous Antiferromagnetic Hall Effect (AHE) conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$), splitting of exciton resonances, Faraday rotation ($	heta_F$), and ellipticity ($	heta_E$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dependence on the magnetization orientation angle $\varphi$ via a $\cos 3\varphi$ term is crucial for diagnostics.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The magnetic layer interaction is treated perturbatively to derive the effective $k\cdot p$ model, and certain exchange interactions are neglected for simplification.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Brillouin zone folding due to magnetism, energy dispersion curves for pristine TMD bands, and theoretical predictions for magneto-optical responses.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the physical system and Hamiltonian (tight binding $ightarrow k\cdot p$ model) to calculating transport properties (AHE via Berry curvature) and finally analyzing optical response (exciton splitting and polarization measurements).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We consider the proximity effects of a commensurate chiral $120^{\circ}$ Néel magnetic structure on the transport and optical properties of a transition metal dichalcogenide monolayer (TMD ML). The enlarged magnetic unit cell leads to the folding of the Brillouin zone and enables efficient intervalley spin-flip scattering. Starting from a six band tight binding model, we develop an effective $k\cdot p$ model, which describes the coupling between charge carriers in the TMD ML and the chiral magnetization. We predict the anomalous antiferromagnetic Hall effect (AHE) for conduction electrons and describe it accounting for the interplay between anomalous velocity, side jump, and skew scattering contributions. The proximity of the chiral magnetization also leads to the mixing and splitting of the exciton resonances in the two valleys which are related by the time reversal symmetry despite zero net magnetization. Finally, we demonstrate the possibility to measure the distribution of in-plane orientation of the chiral magnetization through Faraday rotation and the ellipticity of incident linearly polarized light.

</details>

**Summary.** This research demonstrates that strain engineering offers a powerful tool to control exciton dynamics in WSe2 monolayers. By applying tensile or compressive strain, researchers can modify the energy landscape and suppress specific phonon scattering channels. This manipulation results in an abrupt enhancement of hot dark exciton excess energy and significantly accelerates transient exciton diffusion, paving the way for tailored 2D semiconductor devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides quantitative rules for manipulating quantum transport properties (exciton diffusion) in 2D materials by external mechanical fields (strain), which is highly relevant to designing next-generation optoelectronic devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how strain engineering can precisely control the transient exciton diffusion and energy landscape within WSe2 monolayers at cryogenic temperatures.

**Main result.** Tensile strain above a critical threshold ($s > s_0$) abruptly increases hot dark exciton excess energy, leading to an accelerated transient diffusion coefficient. Compressive strain is predicted to induce periodic modulation of this diffusion via M-phonon emission.

**Method.** The work combines theoretical modeling using master equations for excitonic dynamics with experimental measurements of time- and energy-resolved photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy under controlled uniaxial strain.

**Model / system.** The physical system is WSe2 monolayers encapsulated by hBN, focusing on the interplay between bright and dark exciton states. The dynamics are modeled using an excitonic intravalley Wigner function governed by a master equation that includes spatial evolution, radiative losses, and strain-dependent exciton-phonon scattering terms.

**Key observables.** Transient PL spectrum ($I_s(E, \mathbf{r}, t)$), effective diffusion coefficient $D_s(t)$, and the excess energy of hot excitons ($\langle E_s angle_t$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Strain magnitude ($s$), critical strain threshold ($s_0 \approx 0.3\%$), cryogenic temperatures (20 K, 50 K), and phonon energies (M phonons).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis focuses on the lowest 1s states of specific exciton complexes ($	ext{KK}$, $	ext{K}\Lambda$, $	ext{KK}'$) and uses a Markov approach for scattering dynamics.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate how tensile strain causes spectral reordering, leading to faster transport by deactivating certain scattering channels; another figure shows the abrupt enhancement of $D_s(t)$ above $s_0$ with temperature dependence.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the effect of strain on exciton energy levels (via Wannier equations), models the resulting changes in scattering rates using a master equation, and quantifies the impact on measurable observables like PL spectra shifts and diffusion coefficients ($D_s(t)$).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Tungsten-based transition metal dichalcogenides exhibit dark excitons as the energetically lowest states. These are crucial for exciton thermalization and propagation and they dominate low-temperature photoluminescence via the emergence of pronounced phonon sidebands. After a resonant excitation, highly mobile hot dark excitons are formed, which quickly thermalize into an equilibrium distribution. The application of strain modifies the exciton energy landscape and, in particular, the relative energy separation between bright and dark exciton states. The impact of strain on the transient photoluminescence and diffusion of non-equilibrium excitons has remained largely unexplored so far. In this work, we investigate the spatiotemporal exciton dynamics in strained hBN-encapsulated WSe2 monolayers at cryogenic temperatures. We demonstrate that tensile strain abruptly increases the excess energy of hot excitons, thereby accelerating their transient diffusion. We trace this back to suppressed phonon-mediated scattering from bright to dark excitons. Furthermore, we predict a periodic modulation of the transient exciton diffusion in the presence of a compressive strain resulting from strain-driven emission of M phonons. The gained microscopic insights illustrate how strain can be used to engineer transient photoluminescence and exciton diffusion in technologically promising 2D semiconductors.

</details>

**Summary.** This work presents a novel, ambient-condition Raman characterization technique for graphene-protected bismuthene monolayers. By tuning the excitation laser near the material's excitonic resonance, the researchers revealed intrinsic lattice dynamics and higher-order phonon modes previously inaccessible. This establishes Raman micro-spectroscopy as a powerful tool for probing delicate quantum materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter spectroscopy, the study's emphasis on resonant enhancement mechanisms—where external energy tuning reveals hidden coupling strengths (exciton-phonon)—is highly relevant to understanding light-matter interaction in quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is developing reliable, ambient-condition characterization methods for highly sensitive two-dimensional quantum spin Hall insulators like bismuthene.

**Main result.** The study successfully characterizes graphene-capped bismuthene using ex situ Raman spectroscopy, identifying intrinsic phonon modes and demonstrating resonant enhancement effects linked to excitonic transitions.

**Method.** The research combines experimental techniques (spatially resolved, polarization-dependent Raman spectroscopy) with theoretical calculations (DFPT for phonons, BSE/GW for excitons).

**Model / system.** The system under study is a heterostructure: bismuthene monolayer encapsulated by graphene on an SiC substrate. Bismuthene acts as the quantum spin Hall insulator layer.

**Key observables.** Pronounced Raman scattering peaks (e.g., $122 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$ for bismuthene), resonant enhancement of spectral features, and observation of interlayer breathing modes ($S1$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Excitation energy tuned near the excitonic transition ($\sim 1.58 	ext{ eV}$); high crystalline order (narrow FWHM $\approx 5 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that resonant enhancement is governed by exciton-mediated scattering, and initial theoretical models neglect the weak van der Waals coupling of graphene.

**Figures summary.** Figures show STEM/STM confirmation of structure, Raman spectra mapping B, G, and 2D modes; phonon dispersion curves from DFPT; and absorption spectra showing A and B excitons.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the structural feasibility (STEM/STM), then identifying intrinsic vibrational signatures via standard Raman measurements, and finally utilizing resonant excitation to probe higher-order, exciton-coupled scattering processes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Two-dimensional quantum spin Hall insulators based on atomic monolayers offer a promising route toward dissipationless electronics, yet their practical use is often limited by environmental instability. Encapsulating the system with a graphene capping layer has been shown to be a reliable method to prevent oxidation and degradation. However, the confirmation of a successful encapsulation still relies on ultra-high vacuum techniques, that considerably slow the process. Here, we present an ex situ, rapid, nondestructive and spatially resolved Raman characterization of graphene-capped bismuthene, a honeycomb monolayer of Bi on SiC. A pronounced Raman scattering peak at around 122 cm-1 is identified as the E2g phonon of bismuthene, via a comparison with density functional perturbation theory calculations. We use excitation-energy and polarization-dependent Raman measurements to enable an unambiguous assignment of the spectral features. Tuning the excitation energy close to the excitonic transition in pristine bismuthene, we observe a strong enhancement of the Raman response and the emergence of additional scattering peaks. In this regime, higher-order phonon features, as well as interfacial modes between bismuthene and the SiC substrate, become visible, suggesting the involvement of resonant scattering processes. Our results establish Raman micro-spectroscopy as a versatile tool for probing graphene-protected quantum materials, providing access to lattice dynamics and interlayer coupling.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main result.** The difference in ionic conductivity between metallic and semiconducting CNTs for long tubes is attributed to the time scale required for the internal electric field to dissipate; semiconductors retain a measurable internal field longer than metals.

**Method.** The authors combine theoretical derivations based on quantum mechanical models (calculating electron concentrations and charge) with analysis of experimental measurements concerning ion flow rates under applied fields.

**Model / system.** The system involves metallic and semiconducting carbon nanotubes subjected to an external electric field, where ion transport ($	ext{K}^+$) is measured. The theory models the time evolution of surface charge distribution on the nanotube walls.

**Key observables.** Ionic conductivity, $	ext{K}^+$ flow rates, internal electric field strength ($E$), and characteristic time scales ($	au_t$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Nanotube diameter (2.6-5.4 nm), length (100 $\mu$m vs 11 nm), applied electric field, and electronic parameters like band gap ($g$) and Fermi level ($E_F$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on comparing different time scales: short tubes reach equipotential quickly, while long semiconducting tubes maintain a significant internal field for extended periods.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the electronic charge distribution on metallic nanotubes; Figure 2 sketches the experimental setup used in related literature (Ref. [11]).

**Paper structure.** The paper reviews conflicting literature results regarding ion flow rates, develops a theoretical framework based on charge relaxation times ($	au_t$), and uses this time scale difference to explain why semiconducting tubes exhibit higher conductivity than metallic ones under certain measurement conditions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Measurements made by Li, et. al., showed that the flow rates of potassium ions through 11nm long, subnanometer diameter, metallic and semiconducting carbon nanotubes under an applied electric field are almost the same. In contrast, measurements of the electrical conductivity of potassium chloride solution through 100 long metallic and semiconducting carbon nanotubes with diameters between 2.6-5.4nm by Cui, et. al., show that the ionic conductivity in the semiconducting nanotubes is larger than that of the metallic nanotubes. Possible theoretical origins of these differences are explored in this article.

**Summary.** This theoretical work develops a formalism to study how ferroelectricity and superconductivity can coexist in noncentrosymmetric metals. By treating polarization fluctuations as an effective attractive interaction, the authors derive conditions under which these lattice distortions drive electron pairing, extending BCS theory into polar materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter pairing mechanisms, the treatment of fluctuating order parameters (polarization) mediating interactions is relevant to open quantum systems where environmental coupling drives collective excitations and emergent correlations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work investigates the fundamental physical problem of how superconductivity can coexist with, or even emerge from, ferroelectric ordering in noncentrosymmetric metals.

**Main result.** Superconductivity can be induced by attractive electron-electron interactions mediated by polarization fluctuations, leading to a BCS-type pairing mechanism analogous to phonon mediation.

**Method.** The authors employ a microscopic field-theoretic approach, deriving an effective Hamiltonian by integrating out ionic degrees of freedom (phonons) from the coupled electron-ion system.

**Model / system.** The model is a coupled electron-ion system described by a general Hamiltonian incorporating electronic operators and ionic position/momentum operators. The analysis proceeds via normal mode quantization of the ion subsystem, leading to an effective attractive interaction term for electrons.

**Key observables.** Superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$), superconducting gap ($\Delta$), spontaneous polarization, and the BCS-type gap equation.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The strength of the phonon-mediated attraction relative to Coulomb repulsion; parameters governing ferroelectric order (e.g., displacement magnitude).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Significant approximations are made, including reducing the model to a single relevant band and neglecting odd-order anharmonic couplings in the ion dynamics expansion.

**Figures summary.** The paper illustrates four representative qualitative regimes of pairing enhancement/suppression based on varying coupling strengths and polar dependencies (e.g., enhanced vs. suppressed pairing).

**Paper structure.** The structure moves from defining a general microscopic Hamiltonian for coupled electron-ion dynamics, through normal mode analysis of the ionic subsystem, to deriving simplified BCS gap equations that quantify the conditions for ferroelectric superconductivity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

It has recently been shown in experiments that certain materials can display both superconductivity and ferroelectricity, contrary to a long-standing conjecture that these two phenomena are incompatible, or at least unrelated. In this work we study superconductivity in ferroelectric metals, using a formalism of ionic polarization fields coupled to itinerant electrons, both of which are treated at the microscopic level. The ferroelectric order manifests as a spontaneous polarization that may be uniform or spatially modulated, and fluctuations of the polarization mediate interactions between the electrons. The polarization fluctuations give rise to attractive interactions that can lead to Cooper pairing in certain lattice configurations, analogous to the nonpolar phonons in conventional BCS theory. Working with a simplified BCS model, we derive conditions under which superconductivity can coexist with and even emerge from ferroelectricity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analytically determines the charge density profile inside a superconducting vortex core by simplifying the Bogoliubov–de Gennes equations. It shows that while the bound states create local modulations, global charge neutrality forces extended states to compensate this charge. The final result is a persistent, sign-alternating ripple modulation dictated by screening inefficiency at large momentum transfers.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on superconductivity, the rigorous mathematical techniques developed for solving the screened Poisson equation ($
abla^2 - k_{TF}^2$) using complex envelopes and separation of variables are highly valuable tools applicable to analyzing charge screening in other quantum many-body systems or interfaces.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To provide an elementary analytical account of the charge density profile within a superconducting vortex core, specifically addressing the sign change and residual modulation observed in self-consistent calculations.

**Main result.** The bound-state charge does not integrate to zero; neutrality requires extended states to compensate it exactly, leaving a persistent, sign-alternating $2k_F$ modulation outside the core.

**Method.** Analytical derivation using the slow-mode ansatz applied to Bogoliubov–de Gennes equations, followed by solving the screened Poisson equation using advanced mathematical techniques like separation of variables and 'replacement tricks'.

**Model / system.** The system is a weak-coupling s-wave superconductor containing a single vortex line. The physics is governed by quasiparticle bound states derived from Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) equations, analyzed using a step-like gap profile.

**Key observables.** Charge density profile $\delta n(r)$, potential $\phi(r)$, and the residual $2k_F$ modulation amplitude.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Fermi wavevector ($k_F$), coherence length ($\xi$), Fermi momentum ($E_F$), and the ratio of superconducting gap to Fermi energy ($\Delta_\infty/E_F$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on approximating the normalization constant as weakly dependent on angular momentum, and later uses 'replacement tricks' or separation of variables which are shown to fail near boundaries.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare exact Bessel solutions to approximations for mode normalization; another figure compares numerical vs. analytical solutions for a screened potential source using different mathematical techniques.

**Paper structure.** The paper first derives the in-core density profile analytically using simplified BdG sums, then tackles the screening problem by solving the Poisson equation, comparing several approximation methods (like the replacement trick) against exact solutions to validate the final result regarding residual oscillations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculations have long shown that solving the Poisson equation inside a superconducting vortex turns a one-signed charge depletion into a modulation that alternates in sign with period $π/k_F$. We give an elementary account of that result. Taking the Caroli-de Gennes-Matricon bound states in a step-like gap, we show that the normalization of the bound-state spinor is nearly independent of angular momentum, which collapses the mode sum into closed form. Inside the core the vortex winding removes one Bessel channel from a completeness sum, so the density vanishes on the vortex line and carries Friedel-like oscillations of wavevector $2k_F$; outside it the sum gives a $1/r$ envelope decaying over a coherence length, with a residual ripple. The bound-state charge does not integrate to zero, so neutrality obliges the extended states to compensate it exactly. That compensation is complete at long wavelength but fails at the diameter of the Fermi circle, and what survives is a sign-alternating $2k_F$ modulation reduced only by $4k_F^2/(4k_F^2+k_{TF}^2)$, a factor lying between one-half and three-quarters for any metal. The oscillation is therefore not a delicate effect but a consequence of neutrality and the inefficiency of screening at large momentum transfer: in the screened total the smooth terms cancel and only the ripple is left.

</details>
